exp.0:3:
This verse says that King Ahasuerus wanted to show the riches of the glory of his kingdom and the splendor of his great power. He did so over many days: one hundred and eighty, that is, about six months.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, telling what King Ahasuerus did (many identify him with Xerxes I of Persia, although the text does not say so). He was in Susa, the capital, and he gathered his princes, servants, and governors. The account presents human power in all its brilliance, and so it sets the stage for what will happen next with Esther.

For today: it is easy to impress others with what we have or achieve. This passage invites us to ask what we boast in and what we trust. Human kingdoms, however great they seem, pass away. Let us instead seek the glory that comes from God and live with humility.
exp.0:5:
This verse describes how the place of the king's feast was decorated. There were hangings of white, green, and dark blue, fastened with cords of fine linen and purple to silver rings and marble pillars. The couches, that is, the couches on which the guests reclined, were of gold and silver. The floor was a mosaic of precious stones, such as porphyry, marble, and alabaster.

The narrator of the book tells this to show the enormous wealth of King Ahasuerus (Xerxes) in his palace at Susa. The banquets were meant to display his power before nobles and people. Here it sets the scene for the events that follow in the story.

For today: human beauty and luxury impress us, but they pass away. We can enjoy what God gives us without placing our security in it, and remember that He works even behind scenes of great power.
exp.0:10:
What it says: King Ahasuerus, merry with wine, orders that Queen Vashti be brought before him wearing the royal crown. He wants to display her beauty before the peoples and the princes, because she was lovely to look on.

Context: The speaker is the king, on the seventh day of a great feast. Vashti was holding a separate feast of her own, for the women. He gives the order through seven eunuchs, or court officials. The text does not say exactly how she was supposed to appear, and some think it meant only with the crown, though this is an interpretation. What is clear is that he treated her as something to be shown off.

For today: People are worth more than their appearance or what they add to our image. Let us ask God for a heart that respects others, especially when we have power and decisions are made with a clouded mind.
exp.0:11:
This verse tells that Queen Vashti refused to come when the king sent for her through his eunuchs (court officials). "To come" here means to present herself before someone. The king became very angry, and his anger burned within him, meaning he was filled with fury.

The narrator relates what happened on the seventh day of a great banquet, when King Ahasuerus was merry with wine. He wanted Vashti to come wearing her crown to show her beauty to everyone. The text does not explain why she refused, and for that reason various interpretations have been given. What we do see is the king's reaction, which sets up what follows in the story.

For today: when something upsets or hurts us, it is wise to pause before acting. Anger that runs unchecked, especially in the midst of excess, often leads to decisions we later regret. Let us ask God for calm and wisdom.
exp.0:12:
This verse says that King Ahasuerus, angry because Queen Vashti had refused to come, consulted the wise men. These were men who "knew the times," that is, they understood the periods of history and matters of the law. The text makes clear that the king had the custom of consulting experts in law and judgment before deciding.

The narrator of the book explains this custom in the middle of the story. The king is furious and wants an official answer. The seven princes of Persia and Media, who are close to him, will give him counsel. Some scholars think that "knew the times" refers to knowing precedents, or even to astrologers, but the text does not specify this.

For today: asking for counsel is wise, but it is good to do so calmly. Ahasuerus asked for advice while angry, and that may have influenced what was decided. Before deciding something important, slow down, pray, and seek out wise and just voices.
exp.0:14:
Here the king asks his advisers what the law requires be done with Queen Vashti. She did not carry out the king's command, which had been sent to her through the chamberlains, who were trusted officials at the court. Asuerus is Ahasuerus, and Vasti is Vashti.

The king speaks with seven princes of Persia and Media, wise in the law and the times, who were close to him. Vashti had refused to appear before the king during a banquet. The text does not explain why she refused, so we should not invent a reason. The king, angry, seeks legal counsel.

For today: before reacting in anger, it is wise to seek wise counsel and think about the consequences. Here the question sounds calm, but the decision that follows is harsh. Let us ask God for humility and self-control.
exp.0:15:
Memucan speaks before the king and the princes. He says that Queen Vashti has wronged not only the king, but also all the princes and all the peoples in the provinces of the kingdom. The word "wrong" here is used in the sense of having done an injury or a serious offense against the authority.

Memucan was one of the seven counselor princes. The king asked for their opinion about what to do with Vashti, who refused to come before him. Memucan exaggerates the matter, turning a conflict within the royal household into a threat to the whole empire. The text does not say whether his motive was sincere or whether he was trying to protect his own position, so it is best not to claim either.

For today: let us be careful not to enlarge problems with exaggerated words. Advice given out of fear or pride can lead to hasty decisions. Before we speak, let us ask God for wisdom, and speak with truth and calm.
exp.0:16:
It says that what Queen Vashti did would become known among all the women of the kingdom. According to the counselor, they would begin to look with little respect on their husbands, saying: "The king commanded Vashti to be brought in, and she did not come."

The speaker is Memucan, one of the princes of King Ahasuerus. Vashti had refused to appear before the king and his guests during a great feast. Memucan turns a personal matter into a danger for the whole kingdom. Some think he was exaggerating to flatter the king and to protect the men in power. Here the Bible simply recounts what happened without necessarily approving his advice.

For today: before reacting with anger or fear, it is wise to pause and think. The advice of those who seek their own benefit may sound wise, but it is not always just. Let us ask God for humility and good judgment.
exp.0:18:
Memucan proposes to the king an official decree: that it be written among the laws of Persia and Media, so that it cannot be changed. The decree would be that Vashti must never again come before King Ahasuerus, and that the king give her royal position to another woman who is better than she is.

The speaker is Memucan, one of the king's advisers. Vashti refused to appear at the banquet, and he fears that other wives will do the same and that there will be disrespect in households. This is his own opinion, and the text does not present it as wise counsel from God. It is a political reaction, shaped by wounded pride and fear.

For today: when someone offends us or challenges us, let us not make decisions driven by pride or fear. Before acting, let us pray and ask for wisdom. God invites us to seek respect through love and good example, not through control.
exp.1:1:
These are the words of the king's servants, the officials who attended him. They gave him a proposal: that young unmarried women be sought out, who were lovely to look at, so that he could choose among them.

The one speaking is the group of advisers of King Ahasuerus (Xerxes). His anger at Queen Vashti had already cooled, but she had been removed from her position, and the king kept remembering what had happened. The advisers suggested a remedy: look for a new queen. Here the Bible simply reports the events; it neither approves nor condemns this system, which today strikes us as unjust to women.

For today: before acting on impulse or pain, it is wise to pause and seek wise counsel. And even when the decisions of others are unjust, God can work within them, as the story of Esther will show.
exp.1:2:
This verse is part of the advice that the king's servants give to Ahasuerus. They propose that the king appoint officers in all the provinces to gather the young virgins of fair appearance, that is, of beautiful look. They would be brought to Shushan, the city where the king resided, to the house of the women. There they would be placed under the care of Hegai, a eunuch (a court official) in charge of the women. They would also be given what was needed for their personal preparation.

The servants speak after the king's anger against Vashti, who had been removed, had calmed down. They seek to replace her and, at the same time, to please the king. This was a custom of the Persian court; the text describes it, but it does not say that God approves of it.

For today: God can work even in unjust or cold environments, without everything that happens being good. Trust that he cares for his people, even when we do not yet see how.
exp.1:5:
The verse says that Mordecai, the Jew who lived in Susa, had been carried away from Jerusalem along with the captives whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon deported together with Jeconiah, king of Judah. Being carried away by force to another place is what the verse describes, and the captives are the prisoners taken in war.

The one who speaks is the narrator of the book, who introduces Mordecai by explaining where his family comes from. There is a detail that can be understood in two ways: some think the exile was Mordecai himself, and others think it was his great-grandfather Kish, because the years do not fit well. The text does not fully settle the matter.

For today: God can use people who live far from their land and their comfort. If you feel out of place, your situation is not an obstacle to God working through you.
exp.1:6:
This verse tells how Mordecai raised his cousin Hadassah, also called Esther, because she had been left an orphan. It says she was a young woman of fair form and good appearance, that is, pleasing in figure and face. When her parents died, Mordecai took her as his own daughter. Hadassah is her Hebrew name; Esther is the name by which she became known afterward.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, and his name is not given. He introduces Esther before she is taken to the palace. Both are Jews living in Susa, far from their homeland, descendants of those carried into exile in Babylon. The text does not explain every detail, but it shows that Esther did not come to that situation alone.

For today: God can use those who lovingly care for others without being their parents. Think of someone who needs your support, and help them with steadiness and tenderness.
exp.1:7:
This verse tells us that when King Ahasuerus gave the command to gather many young women in Shushan, the capital city, Esther was also taken into the palace. She was placed under the care of Hegai, the official in charge of the king's women.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, and he does not mention God, but he shows how Esther, a young orphaned Jewish woman raised by her cousin Mordecai, arrives at a place of power. The text does not say whether she went of her own will or by compulsion; interpreters understand it in different ways. What is clear is that the story is preparing her later role.

For today: sometimes we find ourselves in places we did not choose. Even there, God can work quietly, and we can live with wisdom, trusting that our lives have a purpose.
exp.1:11:
This verse tells us that each young woman had to spend twelve months in preparation before she could be presented to King Ahasuerus. For six months they used oil of myrrh, a fragrant oil, and for the other six months they used sweet odours and other things for purifying and beautifying. The young women are the maids, and the preparation itself is the beautifying process.

It is the narrator of the book who explains the custom of the Persian court. After Ahasuerus put Queen Vashti away, they gathered many young women so that another queen could be chosen. Mordecai, Esther's cousin and guardian, watched from a distance over how she was doing, and he had asked her not to reveal her Jewish origin. The text gives no further details about the process.

For today: God works within long processes and situations we did not choose. Esther waited, and later her position would help save her people. We can trust that God uses our times of waiting, even when we cannot yet see the purpose.
exp.1:12:
When it was each young woman's turn to go in to the king, she could ask for whatever she wanted to take with her. Everything was given to her. The verse also explains that a young woman is a maiden, and that the place in the palace where they were prepared was the house of the women.

It is the narrator of the book who describes the process of choosing the new queen, after Vashti was removed. The young women spent a year in preparation. The text does not explain what they asked for or why; we do not know for certain. Later on it becomes clear that Esther asked for nothing, but followed the advice of Hegai, and won the favor of everyone.

For today: we do not always win by having more, but by having a simple and humble heart. We can ask ourselves whether we are seeking to impress others, or whether we trust the guidance of wise people while God works quietly.
exp.1:14:
This verse tells us that the turn came for Esther to present herself before the king. She was the daughter of Abihail, the uncle of Mordecai, who had taken her in and raised her as his own daughter. Esther did not ask for anything special; she simply accepted what Hegai, the chamberlain in charge of the women, advised her. And everyone who saw her came to think well of her.

It is the narrator of the book who speaks. Esther is in the palace of King Ahasuerus, within a long process of choosing a new queen. Other young women asked for ornaments and things to make a good impression, but she acted with simplicity and trust in the advice of someone who knew how the process worked. The book does not explain why she pleased everyone; it simply presents it.

For today: it is not always necessary to appear more than others. Humility, knowing how to listen, and accepting good advice can open doors and leave a good impression without forcing anything.
exp.1:15:
This verse tells that Esther was taken to the royal palace of King Ahasuerus, that is, Xerxes in other versions. It happened in the tenth month, called Tebeth, which roughly corresponds to December or January, in the seventh year of his reign.

It is the narrator of the book who speaks, and he gives precise dates to place the event. Esther had already gone through a period of preparation with the other young women. Earlier it is said that she won the favor of everyone who saw her and that she followed only what Hegai advised her. This moment leads to the next verse: the king makes her queen.

For today: Esther did not rush or seek to impose herself; she acted with humility and patience. We can trust that God works in times that seem slow, and meanwhile live with simplicity and good character.
exp.1:18:
When the young women were gathered together a second time, Mordecai was sitting at the king's gate. The word "virgins" here refers to the young women gathered for the palace. "Was sitting" means that he had a place or position there.

It is the narrator of the book who speaks. Esther is already queen, but Mordecai still remains close to the palace. Scholars do not fully agree on why there was a second gathering of young women. It is also not certain what his exact role at the gate was; many think he held some official position, since the gate was a place where legal matters were handled. What follows shows that he was paying attention to what was happening.

For today: God can work through people who remain faithful in their place, without seeking applause. Mordecai did not take advantage of Esther being queen. He keeps doing his work with constancy. You too can serve faithfully where you are, trusting that God sees and uses what is simple.
exp.1:20:
In those days, while Mordecai was sitting at the king's gate, two of the king's officials, Bigthan and Teresh, who guarded the entrance, became angry and plotted to kill King Ahasuerus.

Laying hands on the king meant attacking him to harm him. The officials who served the king in his court were the ones who attended the palace. The king's gate was a place of daily work and public business, and it is thought that Mordecai held some position there, although the text does not state this clearly.

The narrator tells this event briefly. He does not explain why the guards became angry. Mordecai learned of the plan and warned Esther, who told the king. Everything was written down in the records of the kingdom, and later that record will play a great role in the story.

For today: do what is right even when no one notices or thanks you. Mordecai acted with honesty and loyalty, and God was able to use that act at the right time. Serve faithfully today.
exp.2:0:
After these things, King Ahasuerus advanced Haman, the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, and raised his position, setting his seat above all the princes who were with him. This verse tells us that the king gave Haman a great promotion, honoring him and giving him power and authority, and that Haman was placed in the highest position, above the other officials of the kingdom.

Here the narrator of the book simply reports the events. Esther does not explain why the king chose Haman. What follows shows that this promotion sets up the conflict with Mordecai, who did not bow down to him. That Haman is described as an Agagite could point to a link with Agag, king of the Amalekites, an ancient enemy of Israel, though some scholars debate how much weight that detail carries.

For today: power and applause can grow very quickly, but they do not make anyone good. Let us ask God for humility so that we do not depend on human recognition.
exp.2:3:
This verse says that the king's servants kept urging Mordecai every day to obey the order to bow before Haman, but he would not listen to them. So they reported to Haman, to see whether Mordecai would stand firm in his decision, since he had already told them he was a Jew. The word used for "told" in the verse means that they informed on him, which is to say they reported him.

This is the narrator of the book speaking. Haman was the highest-ranking man in the kingdom, and the king had commanded that everyone kneel before him. Mordecai refused. The text does not explain his reason in detail; it only says that he is a Jew. Some think it was a matter of his faith, but the text does not make this clear.

Today it teaches us that holding to our convictions can bring constant pressure. Let us ask God for wisdom and steadfastness to act with integrity, without seeking conflict, trusting that he cares for his own.
exp.2:5:
He thought it too little to lay hands only on Mordecai. Since he already knew that Mordecai was a Jew, Haman decided to destroy all the Jews in the kingdom of Ahasuerus. Laying hands on someone means raising a hand against them to do them harm. Sought to destroy means that he looked for a way to accomplish it.

The book of Esther tells this from the narrator's point of view. Mordecai would not bow down before Haman, the king's high official, and Haman was filled with rage. His personal anger grew until it became a plan against a whole people. The text does not explain in detail why Mordecai would not kneel; some think it was for reasons of faith, but the Bible does not clarify this here.

Today, this verse warns us that wounded pride and resentment, if they are not stopped, can grow until they harm many people. When we feel offended, let us bring that anger to God quickly, before it leads us to do something unjust.
exp.2:7:
Haman speaks to King Ahasuerus and describes the Jews as a people scattered and divided among all the provinces. He says their laws are different, that they do not keep the king's laws, and that for this reason it is not good for the king to let them live.

Haman speaks out of hatred toward Mordecai and his people. He does not name them: he says "a certain people" without saying which one. He mixes a half-truth (the Jews had customs of their own) with an exaggerated accusation (that they did not obey the king). In this way he seeks to have the king sign a decree without investigating.

For today: let us be wary of those who describe an entire group with generalizations and suspicions. Before repeating or believing an accusation, let us ask for the facts and treat each person with justice, remembering that God sees and cares for his people even when they seem threatened.
exp.2:8:
Haman asks the king to sign a decree to destroy the Jews. He offers to pay ten thousand talents of silver, an enormous sum, to the men in charge of the king's finances, so that the money will reach the royal treasury.

Haman, a senior official of King Ahasuerus, speaks here. He had already accused the Jews of being different and of not obeying the king. Behind his plan lie hatred and ambition. The text calls him the enemy of the Jews, and he tries to buy the king's decision with money.

For today: be wary of anyone who accuses a whole group of people with broad generalizations and offers money or power as the solution. Ask God for courage to defend the wronged and to speak the truth when others stay silent.
exp.2:10:
Here the king Ahasuerus answers Haman. Some interpret that the king refuses the money as a gesture of courtesy, while others hold that he simply hands it over; the text does not make this clear.

The speaker is King Ahasuerus, who does not know that Esther is a Jew. Haman, angry at Mordecai, had presented the Jews as a dangerous people. The king gives him his ring, which served as the official seal, and so Haman gains the authority to issue a decree of destruction.

Today this reminds us that power used without asking questions or investigating can cause enormous harm. Before repeating accusations against others, or making decisions that affect them, let us seek the truth and think about their dignity as people created by God.
exp.2:11:
Esther 3:12 tells us that the king's scribes were called together on the thirteenth day of the first month. There they wrote down everything Haman commanded. The letters were addressed to the king's lieutenants, to the governors over every province, and to the rulers of every people in every province, each according to its writing and each people in its own language. They were written in the name of King Ahasuerus and sealed with the king's ring.

Haman, a high official, hated the Jews. The king had given him his ring, which served as the official seal, and with it he gave him enormous authority. In this way, the order to destroy the Jews became law of the kingdom, and it could not easily be changed.

For today: words and decisions carry great power, especially when authority is used. If we have influence, let us use it to protect and not to harm. And when we see injustice, let us remember that God is not indifferent, even though his work is not yet visible here.
exp.2:12:
This verse tells that letters were sent by messengers to all the provinces of the kingdom. They ordered that all Jews be destroyed, killed, and wiped out, from the children to the elderly, including the women, in a single day: the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, called Adar. They also allowed the attackers to take their possessions.

The narrator describes what Haman, a high official of King Ahasuerus, did. He was offended because Mordecai, a Jew, would not bow down before him. Haman convinced the king to approve the plan, and the decree was sealed with the royal signet ring, which gave it authority. The book shows the danger that the Jewish people faced in Persia.

Today it reminds us that hatred can hide behind authority and unjust laws. We can reject all prejudice and courageously defend those who are mistreated. We can also trust that God continues to care for his people, even when we cannot see it clearly.
exp.2:13:
This verse says that a copy of the king's decree was published in every province and to all peoples. In this way, everyone would know that they must be ready, or prepared and informed, for that appointed day.

The narrator of the book tells how Haman, a high official, managed to get King Ahasuerus to sign an order to destroy the Jews on the thirteenth day of Adar. The decree was translated into every language and spread so that no one could ignore it. Meanwhile, the king and Haman sat down calmly to drink, but the city of Susa was bewildered and distressed.

For today: evil sometimes seems to advance with order and power, but God does not lose control. When you face injustice or fear, pray, seek wise counsel, and do not remain silent or alone. God can work even when it is not yet visible.
exp.3:0:
Mordecai learns of everything that had happened: the king had signed a decree to destroy the Jews. Then he tears his clothes, puts on rough clothing as a sign of mourning, and covers himself with ashes, signs of deep grief in that time. He goes out through the city crying out loudly, with a strong cry full of bitterness.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Esther. Mordecai was a Jew and the cousin and guardian of Esther, the queen. The decree, promoted by Haman, put all his people in danger throughout the Persian empire. His public reaction shows anguish, and the verses that follow say that many Jews did the same.

For today: when pain or injustice strikes you, you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can express your sadness honestly, and then seek God and act with courage, as Mordecai will do later.
exp.3:1:
This verse says that Mordecai came as far as the entrance of the palace, but he could not go in. At that time no one was allowed to enter the king's gate dressed in sackcloth. Sackcloth was a rough, coarse cloth worn as a sign of mourning or grief.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Mordecai had just learned of the decree that condemned the Jews to death. That is why he showed his distress in public. His grief was so great that it led him to the king's gate, even though the palace, by custom, did not allow signs of mourning.

When something truly hurts us, we do not have to pretend we are fine. We can bring our pain honestly before God and trusted people, and seek help instead of carrying it alone.
exp.3:2:
This verse says that in every province where the king's command and decree arrived, the Jews went into very deep grief. They fasted, they wept, and they lamented. Sackcloth was a rough cloth worn in times of mourning, and ashes were also a sign of sorrow. Many lay in sackcloth and ashes.

This is part of the story of the book of Esther, not a speech. Haman had obtained a decree to destroy the Jews throughout the Persian empire. Mordecai, Esther's cousin and guardian, learned of it and showed his anguish openly. The people did the same in every place. These acts expressed grief and also a plea before God, although the text here does not mention his name.

When news comes that crushes us, we do not have to pretend to be strong. We can weep and pray honestly, and seek out other believers so that we do not carry the pain alone. Often God uses those moments to move us to act, as happened with Esther.
exp.3:3:
She says that Esther's maids and her chamberlains came and told her what was happening with Mordecai. Esther was deeply distressed, and she sent clothing so that he would take off the sackcloth, which was a rough cloth worn as a sign of mourning. But Mordecai did not accept it.

It is part of Esther's story, written in the third person. Mordecai was in public mourning because the king's decree threatened all the Jews. Esther, who lived inside the palace, did not yet know the reason. She wanted to ease his grief with clothing, but he was not looking for a quick comfort: his sorrow had a serious cause.

For today: when someone suffers, we sometimes want to fix the appearance of the problem with something quick. It is wise to listen first, as Esther will do later, and to understand what lies behind the pain before offering solutions.
exp.3:6:
Mordecai told him everything that had happened to him. He also informed him of the sum of silver that Haman had promised to pay into the king's treasuries in order to have the Jews destroyed.

Esther, who was queen but did not yet know the gravity of what had occurred, sends Hathach, a trusted eunuch, to find out why Mordecai was in mourning. Mordecai answers with concrete facts: what had happened and the money Haman had offered. In this way Esther could understand that this was not a simple problem, but a real threat against her people.

For today: when we face a difficult situation or ask for help, it is good to speak with clarity and truth, without exaggerating or hiding anything. Honest information helps others understand and act with wisdom.
exp.3:7:
Here Mordecai hands Hathach a written copy of the decree that was published in Shushan to destroy the Jews. Hathach was to show it to Esther and explain everything to her. In addition, Mordecai charges her to go before the king, make her plea to him, and ask on behalf of her people.

Hathach is a servant of the king, sent by Esther. Mordecai, her cousin and guardian, is in mourning over Haman's decree. He wants Esther to see the proof in writing and understand that the danger is real. As queen, she had access to the king, although approaching him without being called was risky.

For today: when you come across an injustice or a need, do not stay silent or occupied only with your own affairs. Ask whether God has placed you where you can speak, pray, or help, and take the first step with humility.
exp.3:9:
This verse says that Esther spoke to Hathach, the king's attendant who carried messages, and gave him instructions to bring back an answer to Mordecai. Esther does not speak directly with her cousin but through this messenger.

Mordecai had asked Esther to go before the king to plead for her people, the Jews, who were threatened with death by a decree. Esther now begins her reply, and in the verses that follow she explains the danger: entering the king's presence without being called could cost her life.

For today: when God asks us for something difficult, it is natural to feel afraid and to express that fear honestly. Esther did not keep silent or pretend to be brave; she spoke plainly. We can do the same in prayer and with trusted people, and seek counsel before taking the next step.
exp.3:13:
Mordecai tells Esther that if she stays silent at this time, relief and deliverance for the Jews will come from another place, but she and her father's house will be destroyed. Then he asks: "And who knows whether you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this?"

Mordecai, Esther's cousin and guardian, speaks to her because Haman had obtained a decree to destroy the Jews. Esther feared approaching the king without being summoned, since that could cost her life. Mordecai trusts that God will not abandon his people, although the text does not name God.

For today: perhaps God has placed you in your position, job, or family to help someone. Do not wait until everything feels safe; ask in prayer what good you can do today, and do it with courage and humility.
exp.3:14:
This verse tells us that Esther sent a reply back to Mordecai. The verse only announces that she is going to respond, and her actual reply appears in the next verse.

Esther is the queen of Persia, and she is Jewish. Mordecai, her relative who raised her, asked her to speak to the king to save their people from death. Entering the king's presence without being called could cost her her life. She does not answer with an excuse but with a decision, and before she acts she asks that everyone pray and fast.

For today: before making a difficult decision, do not act in a hurry or rely only on your own strength. Seek out other believers who will pray with you, and ask God for courage and wisdom.
exp.4:1:
In this verse, King Ahasuerus saw Queen Esther standing in the inner court of the palace, and he was pleased with her. So he held out the golden scepter that he had in his hand, and Esther came near and touched its tip.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. According to chapter 4, Esther came in without being called, and that could cost her her life. The extended scepter was a sign that the king accepted her. She was doing this to ask for help for her people, the Jews, who were under threat.

For today: when you have to take a hard step for the good of others, prepare yourself, pray, and act with respect and courage. You do not know how others will respond, but God can open doors that seemed closed.
exp.4:4:
Here the king responds at once to Esther's invitation. He tells his servants to hurry, and to call Haman so that he may do what the queen asked. Then the king and Haman go to the banquet that Esther prepared.

The one speaking is King Ahasuerus. Esther had come before him without being called, something that could have cost her her life, but he received her with favor. She did not state her real request right away; first she invited the king and Haman, the enemy of her people. Interpreters often see here Esther's wisdom and patience, although the text does not explain all of her motives.

For today: when we face a difficult situation, we can pray and act with wisdom and patience, without rushing ahead, trusting that God can prepare the right moment.
exp.4:8:
This verse says that Haman left the palace happy and in good spirits, because the queen had invited him to a banquet with the king. But when he saw Mordecai at the king's gate, not standing up or showing him respect, he was filled with anger.

The narrator tells what happened after Esther asked that the king and Haman come to a banquet. Haman was a high official of the kingdom. Mordecai, a Jew, did not bow before him. The Bible does not explain the reason in detail here, so we should not claim more than the text says.

For today: good news can make us glad, but a single resentment can take away our peace. It is worth examining what we allow to grow in our hearts. Let us ask God for humility so that we do not live dependent on the recognition of others.
exp.4:11:
Haman keeps boasting before his friends and his wife. He says that Queen Esther invited no one but him to the banquet she prepared for the king. He was also invited again for tomorrow.

Haman speaks at home, after leaving the banquet. He has just bragged about his wealth, his sons, and his power. He does this to feel important, but the next verse shows that he is bitter because of Mordecai, who will not bow down to him. What Haman does not know is that Esther is preparing something against him.

For today: let us watch over pride. Haman had honor, money, and family, but he had no peace, because his heart was full of resentment. Let us seek humility and give thanks to God, instead of measuring our worth by the approval of others.
exp.4:13:
This verse tells how Zeresh, Haman's wife, and his friends advise him to build a gallows, very tall, fifty cubits high (about 22 meters, roughly). They suggest he ask the king to hang Mordecai on it, and then go cheerfully to the banquet. The word "pleased" in the verse means that Haman liked the idea, and he ordered the gallows to be prepared.

Haman has just boasted of his wealth and honor, but he admits that all of it means nothing to him as long as Mordecai does not bow before him. His wounded pride has turned into hatred. Those around him, instead of calming him, feed his resentment. What Haman does not know is that this gallows will become his own end, as the book will show later.

Today, stored-up resentment can grow until it controls us. Let us ask God for humility and seek counselors who bring us toward peace, not those who stir up our anger. As Proverbs 16:18 says, pride comes before destruction.
exp.5:0:
That night the king could not sleep. He asked for the book of records, meaning the official register of the events of the kingdom, and it was read aloud to him. The phrase about his sleep leaving him means that he had insomnia.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Esther. Just before this, Haman had prepared a gallows for Mordecai, and the Jews were in danger because of a decree of destruction. The text does not explain why the king could not sleep or why he chose that reading. Many believers see here the hand of God acting without being named, although the book does not say so directly.

For today: God can work in small and unexpected details, such as a sleepless night. Trust that, even when you cannot see what He is doing, He has not forgotten you.
exp.5:3:
This verse shows the king, unable to sleep, asking who is in the court. Right there was Haman, who had come early to ask the king's permission to hang Mordecai on the gallows already prepared. Here "gallows" refers to a tall wooden post or pole, and "outer court" was the outer area of the palace.

King Ahasuerus is speaking. That night he could not sleep, and he ordered the book of the chronicles to be read, where it was found that Mordecai had uncovered a plot against his life and had never been rewarded. Haman arrives with his plan of revenge, not knowing that the king is thinking of honoring Mordecai. The two intentions cross at that moment.

For today: even when it sometimes seems that no one sees the good we do, God knows the right moment. We do not have to take revenge or rush things; we can trust that He governs the times and justice.
exp.5:8:
Here Haman tells King Ahasuerus how to honor someone. He asks that a royal robe and one of the king's horses be given to one of the most noble princes, so that he may dress that man and lead him on horseback through the city square. In front of him, a herald will announce that this is how the one whom the king wishes to honor is to be treated.

Haman is speaking, the most powerful man after the king. He believes the king wants to honor him, so he describes the greatest honor he can imagine. But the king was referring to Mordecai, the Jew whom Haman hated. So Haman himself has to do what he proposed.

For today: pride deceives us and makes us seek applause. Better that we serve with humility, trusting that God knows when and how to honor each person.
exp.5:9:
Here the king Ahasuerus orders Haman to carry out at once what Haman himself proposed: take the royal robe and the horse, and honor Mordecai the Jew, who sits at the king's gate.

The king speaks to Haman, who believed the honor would be for himself, and so had described a great distinction. Ahasuerus did not know that Haman hated Mordecai. Shortly before, the king had remembered that Mordecai had never been rewarded for saving his life. Thus Haman is bound to honor his enemy.

For today: it is not worth living to seek applause or to hold on to resentment. Pride can lead us to shame, while God cares for the humble and works even when we do not see it. We can serve faithfully and trust that He knows how to act in His own time.
exp.5:10:
Haman does exactly what the king commanded. He takes the royal robe and the horse, dresses Mordecai, leads him through the street of the city, and proclaims before him that this is how the man the king wishes to honor shall be treated.

The narrator is telling the scene. Haman had believed the king wanted to honor him, and that is why he proposed such a great honor. But the king orders that it be given to Mordecai, the Jew whom Haman hated and wanted to destroy. So Haman is humiliated in front of everyone.

For today: pride and resentment can blind us and turn against us. It is better to learn to recognize the achievements of others without envy, and to trust that God is the one who lifts up and brings down in his own time.
exp.5:11:
After honoring Mordecai through the streets, Mordecai returned to his duties at the king's gate. Haman, on the other hand, ran home full of sorrow and with his head covered.

The narrator recounts this unexpected turn. Haman had planned to hang Mordecai, but the king asked him to publicly honor his enemy. Mordecai is not puffed up by the honor; he remains in his place of service. Haman, humiliated, seeks comfort from his family, who warn him that he is headed for a fall.

For today: when you receive recognition, or when someone else receives it and it hurts you, remember that pride sinks us and humility keeps us steady. God is the one who lifts up and who brings low. Keep doing your duty with simplicity and trust that he cares for your cause.
exp.5:12:
Haman told his wife Zeresh and all his friends everything that had happened to him: he had been made to honor Mordecai in public. His advisers and Zeresh answered him that, if Mordecai is of the seed of the Jews, Haman will not prevail against him, but will surely fall before him.

Haman was humbled, since the king had ordered him to honor his enemy. His advisers and his wife now speak, the same people who had encouraged his pride before. Now they see that something greater is at work. The text does not explain why they think this way; it only shows their fear before the Jewish people. Soon after, Haman is called to Esther's banquet.

Today we can remember that pride and resentment blind us and in the end bring us down. God can change circumstances, and our plans do not control them. It is better to humble ourselves, ask forgiveness, and trust in Him than to struggle against what He is sustaining.
exp.5:13:
While they were still speaking with him, the king's officials arrived and hurried to bring Haman to the banquet that Esther had prepared. The word "prepared" here means arranged or made ready.

Haman had just been humiliated: he had to publicly honor Mordecai, whom he hated. His advisers had warned him that if Mordecai was Jewish, he would not defeat him. He was given no time to think, for he was taken right away to Esther's second banquet, where she would reveal her plan. The account does not mention God, but it shows how everything falls into place at the right time.

For today: even when evil plans seem to be moving forward, God can work in the details and the timing. We can trust in his justice, without seeking revenge or despairing.
exp.6:9:
This verse tells us that Haman was hanged on the very gallows he had set up to kill Mordecai. "Prepared" here means set up or arranged, and the "gallows" was a tall wooden post on which a person was put to death. When this happened, the king's anger was calmed.

The narrator sums up the end of Haman's fall. He had planned to destroy Mordecai and the whole Jewish people. But Queen Esther revealed his plan to King Ahasuerus, and the king, furious, ordered that Haman be hanged. Some see in this an ironic justice; the book does not name God, but it shows how the evil planned against others turns back on the one who devised it.

For today: we do not have to take revenge or live in bitterness when someone wrongs us. We can act with courage and truth, as Esther did, and trust that God knows how to bring about justice in his time (Romans 12:19).
exp.7:3:
Here the king Ahasuerus holds out his golden scepter toward Esther, which was the sign that she could come near and speak without danger. She gets up and stands before him.

The passage describes what happens. Esther had already been weeping at the king's feet, pleading with him to cancel Haman's plan against the Jews. Although Haman had already fallen, his decree was still in force. With the scepter, the king gives her permission to keep speaking, and she will now present her formal request.

For today: when someone with more power opens the door for us, it is wise to speak with respect, courage, and clarity. Esther did not stay silent in the face of her people's suffering. We too can intercede for others with humility and firmness, and pray trusting that God hears us.
exp.7:4:
Esther makes her request to the king with great respect. She speaks as the verse does: "If it please the king, and if I have found favour in his sight, and the thing seem right before the king, and I be pleasing in his eyes." She asks that the letters Haman, the son of Hammedatha, had written to destroy the Jews in all the provinces be reversed.

Queen Esther is the one speaking. Haman had already been hanged, but his decree was still in force, and Persian laws could not easily be cancelled. That is why she comes back, weeping, to plead for her people. The king extends the golden sceptre to show that she may speak.

For today: when someone suffers injustice, it is not enough to be glad that the guilty party has fallen. Esther kept pressing her case with humility, courage and love for her people. We can use whatever voice, influence or prayer we have to stand up for others, trusting that God also works through people who are willing.
exp.7:5:
Esther tells the king that she cannot remain looking on while her people suffer. With grief, she asks how she could bear to see the disaster and ruin of her family and her people. Here "people" refers to her relatives, her Jewish people.

Queen Esther had already come before King Ahasuerus. Haman had obtained a decree to destroy the Jews, and although Haman had already been hanged, that order was still in force. Esther asks that it be overturned, because a king's law could not simply be cancelled.

For today: when someone we love suffers an injustice, we cannot look the other way. If God has given us a voice, influence, or resources, we can use them with respect and courage to help, to pray, and to act on behalf of others.
exp.7:6:
Here the king Ahasuerus reminds Queen Esther and Mordecai the Jew of what he has already done for them: he gave Esther the house of Haman, and Haman was hanged on the gallows because he set out to attack the Jews.

The king is speaking in response to Esther's plea, since she had just begged him with tears to overturn Haman's decree ordering the destruction of all the Jews. The king points to what has already been done, and in the verses that follow he gives them permission to write a new decree. Persian law could not be revoked, so another way out was sought.

For today: when an injustice threatens others, Esther teaches us not to stay silent. We can use with courage and respect whatever influence we have, whether little or much, to defend those who are in danger.
exp.7:7:
Here the king Ahasuerus gives Esther and Mordecai permission to write a new order in favor of the Jews, using the king's authority. The king's ring served as the official seal. An order sealed in this way cannot be revoked: it could not be cancelled.

The king speaks after Haman, the enemy of the Jews, has been executed. Haman had obtained a decree to destroy the Jewish people, and that law could not be cancelled. For this reason the king allows a second order that gives them protection. Esther had pleaded for her people, and Mordecai now receives authority to act.

For today: when you face a problem that seems to have no way out, pray with courage and seek wise solutions. God can open paths you had not imagined.
exp.7:8:
On the twenty-third day of Sivan, the third month, which falls roughly between May and June, the king's secretaries were summoned. There they wrote down everything Mordecai commanded, and the letters were addressed to the Jews and to the officials: the satraps (governors), the captains and the princes of the 127 provinces, from India to Ethiopia. Each letter was written in the language and script of its own people, and also in that of the Jews.

Background: Haman had obtained a decree to destroy the Jews, and that law could not be revoked. So King Ahasuerus gave Esther and Mordecai permission to write a second decree that would allow the Jews to defend themselves.

For today: For a message to reach the heart, it has to be communicated in a way people can understand. Think about how you can explain your faith in simple, close words, without assuming that everyone understands your language.
exp.7:9:
He wrote letters in the name of King Ahasuerus and sealed them with the royal signet ring, which served as the official signature. He sent them by couriers on horseback, riding on mules, camels, and swift young dromedaries, meaning fast animals used in the king's service.

After Haman had plotted to destroy the Jews, the king's first decree could not be revoked. So Esther and Mordecai received permission to write a second decree. This one did not cancel the first, but it allowed the Jews to defend themselves. The text emphasizes urgency: word had to reach every province quickly.

For today: when there is an urgent need, God often uses ordinary means, such as planning, communication, and diligent effort. We can pray in faith and also act wisely to help others in time.
exp.7:10:
This verse says that the king allowed the Jews in every city to gather together and defend their lives. They could destroy and kill any armed force of a people or province that attacked them, including little ones and women, and take their goods as plunder.

Here the text describes the decree of King Ahasuerus, written at the command of Mordecai. Earlier, Haman had obtained a law to wipe out the Jews, and that law could not be revoked. So another decree was issued that allowed them to defend themselves. Some understand the phrase about little ones and women to describe those who would attack them, while others see an expression that reflects the wording of the first decree. Scholars interpret it in several ways.

For today: when you face injustice, look for paths of protection and justice without hatred, trusting that God cares for his people.
exp.7:11:
This verse gives the date on which the Jews could defend themselves: one single day in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus, the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is the month Adar. King Ahasuerus is the Persian king known as Xerxes. Adar was the last month of the Hebrew calendar, falling between February and March.

Mordecai writes in the king's name and seals the letter with the king's signet. Earlier, Haman had obtained a decree to destroy the Jews on that very day, and a decree of the king could not be revoked. So a new decree is issued that allows them to defend their lives. Some readers see in the words about children and women a reply to the first decree; others debate how they should be understood.

God cared for his people even though his name does not appear in the book. Today we can trust that he works in difficult circumstances, even when we do not see him. In the meantime, let us act with courage and wisdom, and do what is within our reach.
exp.7:12:
This verse says that a copy of the king's decree was to be published in every province, so that all peoples would know it. The message was that the Jews were to be ready for that day. They could defend themselves and act against those who attacked them.

King Ahasuerus, through Mordecai and Esther, responds to the earlier decree of Haman, which ordered the destruction of the Jews. Because a Persian law could not be revoked, another was issued that allowed them to defend themselves. The text presents it as a defense of the people's lives. Some readers notice that the language is harsh, and that is understandable within its time and its situation of danger.

For today: when you face a threat or an injustice, do not remain passive, nor act out of hatred. Seek with wisdom the just ways to protect those who depend on you, and trust that God cares for his own.
exp.7:14:
This verse tells how Mordecai came out from the presence of King Ahasuerus dressed like someone of high rank. He wore clothing of blue and white, a great golden crown, and a garment of fine linen and purple. The whole city of Shushan filled with joy.

The narrator describes the change in the situation. Earlier, Haman had obtained a decree to destroy the Jews. Now Haman is gone, and the king honors Mordecai, who had been loyal. A new decree allowed the Jews to defend themselves. That is why the city celebrates.

For today: even when injustice seems to win, God can change situations in his own time. We can keep acting with faithfulness and hope, and rejoice when justice makes its way.
exp.8:0:
It says that on the thirteenth day of the month of Adar, the twelfth month of the Jewish calendar, the time came for the king's decree to be carried out. On that day, the enemies of the Jews expected to gain control over them, but the opposite happened: the Jews gained the upper hand over those who hated them.

The narrator of the book of Esther is speaking. Earlier, Haman had obtained a decree to destroy the Jews throughout the empire. Afterward, Esther and Mordecai obtained another decree that allowed them to defend themselves. This verse shows the turn of the story: what seemed to be a sentence of death ended in protection.

For today: when a situation seems hopeless, do not give up or act in despair. Pray, seek wise counsel, and do what is yours to do with courage and honesty. Although God is not named in Esther, his care is seen in the outcome.
exp.8:1:
It says that on the thirteenth day of Adar, the Jews gathered together in their cities, throughout all the provinces of King Ahasuerus, to defend themselves against those who sought to harm them. To lay hand on such as sought their hurt means to attack or act forcefully against someone. No one could stand against them, because a great fear of them had fallen upon all the peoples.

Here the narrator of the book of Esther speaks. Earlier, Haman had obtained a decree to destroy the Jews on that very day. Since Persian laws could not be revoked, the king allowed the Jews to defend themselves. The account shows how the situation turned completely around.

For today: God can change situations that seem lost. When we face injustice or threats, we can act with courage and wisdom, and trust that God works even when we do not see it directly.
exp.8:2:
This verse says that all the officials of the Persian empire, that is, the governors of the provinces, the viceroys, the captains and the king's officers, supported and favored the Jews. The reason is that the fear of Mordecai, that is, the respect and dread of his power, had fallen upon them.

Here the narrator of the book of Esther is speaking. The 13th day of Adar was the date set for attacking the Jews, but the situation was turned around. Mordecai was already very important at the court of King Ahasuerus, and that is why the officials sided with the Jews.

For today: God can change situations that seem lost, often in unexpected ways. Trust Him when everything seems against you, and humbly use whatever influence He gives you to protect others.
exp.8:8:
This verse continues the list of the ten sons of Haman. The names given here are Parmashta, Arisai, Aridai and Vaizatha. All of them are Persian names.

The narrator of the book of Esther tells what happened when Haman plotted to destroy the Jews. The king allowed them to defend themselves. That defense included Haman's sons, who were part of the threat. The text repeats that they did not take the plunder, and this shows that they did not act for gain. Some scholars think the very detailed list emphasizes that the event was real and official.

For today: when you have to defend what is right, do it with a clean heart. Do not use conflicts to gain personal advantage. Ask God to keep you from greed.
exp.8:10:
That same day, the king Ahasuerus was told how many had been killed in Shushan, the capital, where he lived. The place where the king lived, meaning his palace and main city, is what the verse refers to here. A count, meaning a report or record, is what was brought to him.

The speaker here is not a character but the narrator of the book. The Jews defended themselves against those who wanted to destroy them, according to the decree that Haman had promoted. Haman's ten sons were killed, and the text stresses that the Jews did not take the plunder. This shows that they were acting in self-defense and not for gain. The report to the king opens the conversation with Esther.

For today: when you have to defend what is right, do it with clean motives. Do not let yourself be moved by personal profit, revenge, or the desire to get ahead, but by care for life and for the truth.
exp.8:11:
Here King Ahasuerus tells Queen Esther what he has been informed: in Shushan, the capital, the Jews killed five hundred men and the ten sons of Haman. Then he wonders what has happened in the rest of the provinces, and he offers Esther whatever she asks for.

The king speaks after Haman, an enemy of the Jews, had planned to destroy them. Since the first decree could not be reversed, the king allowed the Jews to defend themselves. Esther receives once again an open offer, and in the next verse she asks for one more day in Shushan. Some readers are troubled by this request, and the text does not fully explain it.

For today: when God places us in a position of influence, it is good to use it with courage and wisdom, asking clearly and keeping in mind the protection of the vulnerable.
exp.8:18:
This verse says that the Jews who lived in villages and towns without walls kept the fourteenth day of the month Adar. For them it was a day of joy, of feasting with food, and of rest. They also sent portions of food to one another. The people of the villages are those who live in the countryside or in small towns, and the towns without walls are settlements that had no protective city walls.

The writer of the book tells how the feast of Purim began. The Jews had defended themselves against those who wanted to destroy them, and God had delivered them. Those in the villages rested on the fourteenth day; those in Susa, the capital, did so on the fifteenth, because they fought one more day there. That is why the dates differ according to the place.

Today we can do something similar: remember with gratitude how God has cared for us and share that joy with others. This week, invite a neighbor or someone who is alone to a meal, or bring them a dish, and tell them something good that God has done for you.
exp.8:19:
Esther 9:20 says that Mordecai wrote down what had happened and sent letters to all the Jews of the kingdom of King Ahasuerus. He did this both to those who lived nearby and to those who lived far away.

The narrator of the book tells how the Jews had been spared from a plan to destroy them. Mordecai, who had risen to a position of influence, wanted no one to forget that deliverance. So he wrote, and in the verses that follow he asks that each year it be celebrated with a feast, joy, gifts to neighbors, and help for the poor.

For today: do not keep silent about what God has done for you. Write it down, share it with others, and let it become gratitude and generosity toward those who most need it.
exp.8:21:
This verse explains what was to be remembered in those days: the time when the Jews rested from their enemies, and the month when their sorrow was turned into joy and their mourning into a good day. Because of this, they were to make those days times of feasting and gladness. They were also to send portions of food to one another, and to give gifts to the poor.

Mordecai, a Jew who became very important in the kingdom of Ahasuerus, writes this letter to the Jews in all the provinces. Their deliverance had just happened: Haman had planned to destroy them, but that plan failed. Mordecai wants them not to forget what happened and to celebrate it every year. This is the story of the feast of Purim.

For today: when God delivers us from something difficult, it is good to remember it with gratitude. But it is not celebrated alone: it is shared with neighbors, and help is given to those in need.
exp.8:23:
This verse explains why the feast of Purim exists. Haman, a descendant of Agag, saw the Jews as enemies and planned to destroy them completely. He cast the lot, a way of deciding something by chance, like rolling dice or drawing lots, to choose the day for his plan.

The narrator of the book of Esther summarizes what happened here, to explain the name of the feast. The Jews had gone from sorrow to joy, and Mordecai asked them to remember that deliverance with feasts, gifts, and help for the poor.

For today: Haman believed that chance would decide the fate of a people, but the outcome was different. We can trust that God cares for his people even when everything seems uncertain. And when we receive relief, let us do as they did: give thanks and share with those in need.
exp.8:29:
This verse says that Mordecai sent letters to all the Jews who lived in the one hundred twenty-seven provinces of King Ahasuerus. The word "letters" means written messages or documents. And "words of peace and truth" means messages of calm and sincerity, not of threat or deception.

The narrator of the book tells how Mordecai and Queen Esther wanted the people to remember their deliverance every year. After having been in danger of being destroyed, they were now asked to celebrate Purim. Mordecai did not impose the feast harshly, but with a peaceful and truthful message. Some scholars see here a tone of reconciliation and unity.

For today: when you have to correct, invite, or remind others of something, do it with words of peace and truth. Being sincere does not have to be harsh, and being kind does not mean keeping silent about the truth.
exp.3:10:
Esther sent word back to Mordecai that everyone in the kingdom knows a strict rule: whoever approaches the king in the inner court without being summoned must be put to death. The only exception is that the king extends the gold scepter toward that person, and then they may live. The scepter is the rod that stands for the king's authority. Esther adds that she has not been summoned to appear before the king for the past thirty days.

Queen Esther is speaking, answering through the messenger Hatach. Mordecai had asked her to plead with the king to save the Jews from the decree of destruction. She explains the real danger that doing so would involve. It is not a clear refusal; it shows her fear and her limits.

For today: when God calls us to do something difficult, we can be honest about our fears, as Esther was. Saying "I am afraid" is not a lack of faith. What matters is not to stop there, but to seek the counsel of other believers and ask God for courage.
exp.2:9:
The verse says that the king removed the signet ring from his finger and gave it to Haman, who is described as "Haman son of Hammedatha, the Agagite" and "the enemy of the Jews." The ring served as a seal: with it the king's orders were signed, and no one could change them.

Haman had just accused the Jews before the king. He presented them as a separate people who did not keep the king's laws, and he offered money to destroy them. The king investigated nothing and gave Haman his authority. Some believe that "Agagite" connects him with Agag, king of the Amalekites, though this is not known with certainty.

For today: before believing an accusation against someone, let us listen calmly and seek the truth. Well-chosen words can hide hatred, and injustice grows when no one asks questions.
exp.4:5:
The verse tells how King Ahasuerus, while they were drinking their wine, asks Esther what she wants. He promises that it will be given to her, and even offers a generous amount: "even up to half the kingdom." The two questions he asks, about her petition and her request, are almost the same idea: what she wishes to ask for.

The king speaks, and he does so for the second time, since he had already made a similar offer before. Esther had come before him without being summoned, which was risky, and he received her with favor. She prepared a banquet and also invited Haman, the enemy of her people. Many understand this waiting of Esther as prudence: she is looking for the right moment. The Bible does not explain all of her reasons.

For today: before acting in a difficult situation, pray, think, and wait with wisdom. God can guide you to choose the right moment, without rushing or being paralyzed by fear.
exp.0:13:
This verse names seven counselors of King Ahasuerus: Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan. They were princes of Persia and Media. The description that they "had personal access to the king" means they could see him directly, something granted to very few. The description that they "ranked highest in the kingdom" indicates that they held the highest positions.

The narrator of the book explains who the counselors were whom the king consulted. Ahasuerus was furious because Queen Vashti had not obeyed his command. Before acting, he consulted these men, who knew the law and the customs. Shortly afterward, Memucan will be the one who speaks.

For today: having wise counselors close at hand is valuable, but they must be chosen well, and one should seek their advice calmly, not in the middle of anger. Facing a difficult decision, it is wise to pray and listen to prudent voices before acting.
exp.8:25:
This verse explains why the festival is called Purim. The name comes from "Pur," the word for the lot, because Haman cast lots to choose the day to destroy the Jews. The verse goes on to say that the days are kept because of all the instructions in the letter and because of all that the people had seen and experienced.

The narrator of the book tells how the Jews of Persia decided to remember their deliverance. Mordecai and Esther wrote letters to fix the celebration. What Haman planned as destruction, God turned into rescue, although in Esther the name of God does not appear explicitly.

For today: let us not allow the memory of the times we were delivered to be lost. Recording and telling what we have seen and experienced of God's faithfulness strengthens our faith and that of our children.
exp.8:20:
This verse says that Mordecai commanded the Jews to celebrate every year on the fourteenth and fifteenth days of the month of Adar. "Establishing" the celebration means setting it up as a lasting practice, and "celebration" means remembering the event with a feast.

The narrator tells what Mordecai did after the Jews were saved from Haman's plan to destroy them. Mordecai wrote letters to all the provinces of King Ahasuerus's kingdom. Some Jews kept the fourteenth day and others the fifteenth, depending on whether they lived in villages or in walled cities. With this order the aim was to unify the date and keep alive the memory of that deliverance. This is the basis of the feast of Purim.

For today: take some time to remember with gratitude the times God sustained you in difficult moments. You can write them down or share them with your family, and help someone in need, as Mordecai urged.
exp.3:12:
Mordecai tells Esther not to imagine that she will be safe just because she lives in the king's palace. The phrase "do not imagine in your heart" means she should not picture herself as exempt from danger. He warns her that if the decree of destruction is carried out, she would not escape the fate of the other Jews any more than they would.

Esther had just explained that going in to the king without being called could cost her her life. Mordecai, her cousin who raised her, answers her firmly. A decree threatened all the Jews in the kingdom, and he urges her to act. His message is harsh, but it comes from love and from the urgency of the moment.

For today: do not hide behind your comfort or your position when others are suffering and you are able to help. Ask God for courage and wisdom to use your place, your voice, or your influence on behalf of others, even when it involves risk.
exp.6:2:
Esther speaks to the king with respect. She says, "If I have found favor in your sight, O king," that is, if she has his favor, and "if it pleases the king," meaning if it seems good to him. Then she asks for two things: that her life be granted to her, and the lives of her people. "Petition" and "request" are two ways of saying what she asks for.

Esther is the Jewish queen in Persia. She is at the second banquet with King Ahasuerus and Haman. Until now she had kept her origin a secret, but now, risking her life, she reveals that her people are condemned to die by a decree that Haman promoted.

Esther does not accuse in anger, but speaks with humility, clarity and courage. When we must defend others or speak about something unjust, we can do it with respect, with truth, and trusting in God, even if it is frightening.
exp.0:9:
On the seventh day of the banquet, when King Ahasuerus was already cheerful and merry from wine, he gave an order to seven officials who served him closely. These officials were members of the royal court, men who attended the king directly. Here "gave an order" means that he commanded them to do something. The seven are named one by one.

It is the narrator of the book who tells this. The banquet had lasted a full week, and the king had allowed each person to drink as they pleased. What follows shows that he gave the order with his judgment clouded by wine: he wanted to display the beauty of Queen Vashti. The text does not say whether wine was the only cause, but it does mark the moment.

For today: decisions made in a moment of excitement, or under the influence of something that clouds judgment, can bring painful consequences. Before giving an order or speaking with authority, it is wise to pause and think calmly.
exp.1:3:
This verse says that the king's attendants propose a plan: to seek out beautiful young women, and whichever one pleases the king will become the new queen in place of Vashti. The suggestion pleased the king, and he acted on it.

The ones speaking are the attendants of King Ahasuerus, also known as Xerxes. He had grown angry with Vashti because she refused to come when he called for her, and they look for a solution. It is a human plan, made for convenience and power, and many women had no choice in the matter. Here God is not named, but the book will go on to show how his care works quietly.

For today: even when we see unjust or selfish decisions around us, we can trust that God is still at work. In the meantime, let us ask for wisdom to treat others with respect and justice.
exp.2:1:
What it says: All the royal servants at the king's gate bowed down and paid homage to Haman, because the king had commanded that this be done for him. But Mordecai would not bow down or pay homage. Bowing down and paying homage were gestures of honor and deep respect.

Context: The narrator tells how King Ahasuerus had raised Haman above all the princes. The verse does not explain here why Mordecai refused. Some think it was because of his faith, since the gesture seemed like an act of worship. Others connect it to the long-standing enmity between Israel and Amalek, from whom the Agagites may have descended. The following verses only say that Mordecai was a Jew.

For today: Holding firmly to what one believes can be costly and can bring pressure from others. Let us ask God for wisdom to be firm, respectful, and humble, while remaining faithful to Him.
exp.4:3:
Esther answers the king respectfully. She asks him to come today, together with Haman, to a banquet she has prepared for the king. The phrase "if it pleases the king" shows her humble approach, since she is speaking to a ruler who holds power over her life.

Esther has just come before the king without having been called, which could have cost her her life. The king shows her favor and even offers her up to half the kingdom. She does not yet ask for what she truly needs, which is to save her people. Instead, she invites him to a banquet. The Bible does not explain why, but many believe she was waiting for the right moment and acting with caution.

Today we can learn that it is not always wise to rush. Before speaking or acting in difficult situations, it is good to pray, think calmly, and ask God for wisdom to choose the right moment.
exp.4:6:
Esther answers the king here, and she says what she wants to ask of him. "Petition" and "request" mean nearly the same thing, so the two words together stress that she is about to make her appeal. It is as if she were saying, "This is what I want to ask you." But the request itself comes in the next verse.

Esther is at the banquet she prepared for King Ahasuerus and Haman. The king has already offered her up to half the kingdom. She does not respond right away with her great request, but takes one more step: she invites them to a second banquet. The Bible does not explain her reasons; some think she was looking for the right moment, but this is only an interpretation.

For today: not everything is resolved in a hurry. Sometimes it is wise to pray, wait, and act with prudence, trusting that God guides the right moment.
exp.1:22:
This verse tells us that the plot against King Ahasuerus was investigated and confirmed to be true. The two guilty officers were hanged on the gallows, which means they were publicly executed. The matter was also recorded in the Book of the Chronicles, the official record of the kingdom, and it was recorded in the presence of the king. The phrase "after the report had been investigated and verified" means that an inquiry was carried out and the charge was confirmed.

Here the narrator of the book of Esther is speaking. Mordecai had discovered the plan and alerted Esther, and she told the king. This record may seem like a minor detail, but later, in Esther 6, that same book will be read to the king and will bring about an important turn in the story. In this way, without mentioning God, we see how things are gradually falling into place.

For today: do what is right even when no one acknowledges it. God sees what we do in silence, and he can use in his own time what seemed forgotten.
exp.7:1:
This verse says that the king removed the signet ring, the same one he had taken back from Haman, and gave it to Mordecai. Esther also appointed Mordecai over the estate that had belonged to Haman. The words "removed" and "presented" are the actions in the verse, and the phrase "appointed Mordecai over the estate" means that he was made the manager of everything that had belonged to Haman.

This is part of the story of Esther. Haman had planned to destroy the Jews and had already been executed. King Ahasuerus gave Esther the house of Haman, and Esther revealed her kinship with Mordecai. The ring was used to seal decrees with royal authority, so Mordecai received a position of trust. Even so, the danger to the Jews had not yet passed.

For today: God can change unjust situations, but he often expects us to act with courage and wisdom. Let us humbly use any influence we receive to serve and protect others.
exp.1:13:
What it says: Each young woman spent one night with King Ahasuerus. She would go in the evening, and in the morning she would return to a second harem, under the care of Shaashgaz, the king's eunuch in charge of the concubines, that is, the king's secondary wives. She would not return to the king unless he delighted in her and summoned her by name.

Context: This is the account of the narrator of the book of Esther. It explains how the king sought a new queen after Vashti was removed. The scene shows a harsh court system, where women had very little freedom. It prepares the way for Esther's entrance.

For today: God can work in unjust or painful places, even though he does not approve of them. We can trust that he cares for those who live in situations they did not choose, and we can defend the dignity of vulnerable people.
exp.5:5:
This verse tells how Haman comes into the king's presence, and the king asks him what should be done for the man whom the king is delighted to honor. Haman thinks to himself: "Whom would the king be delighted to honor more than me?" The word "honor" here means public recognition and respect.

The narrator speaks, and then King Ahasuerus and Haman. That night the king could not sleep, he read the records and discovered that Mordecai had saved his life without receiving any reward. Haman had come to ask for Mordecai's death, but without knowing it, the king wants to honor exactly that man.

For today: pride makes us believe that all praise is for us, and it blinds us to what God is doing. We can ask him for a humble heart, one that rejoices when others are recognized and does not always seek to be the center.
exp.8:16:
This verse says that the thirteenth day of the month Adar was the day when the Jews in the provinces defended themselves against their enemies. On the fourteenth day they rested, and they made it a day of feasting and joy.

Here the narrator of the book of Esther tells how God protected his people in the Persian empire. A decree had ordered the Jews destroyed, but another decree allowed them to defend themselves. Once the threat had passed, they rested and celebrated. The verses that follow explain that the people of Susa celebrated a day later, on the fifteenth, and that is why there were two dates of celebration. This is connected to the origin of the feast of Purim.

For today: when God brings us out of a difficult trial, it is good to stop, rest, give thanks, and celebrate with others. Sharing joy with family and friends helps us remember his care for us.
exp.7:2:
This verse tells that Esther came again before King Ahasuerus. She fell at his feet, wept, and begged him to revoke the evil scheme that Haman the Agagite had planned against the Jews.

Haman had already been punished, and his property had been given to Esther. But the decree he had made to destroy the Jews was still in force. Esther was no longer speaking only for her own life, but for her whole people. That is why she pleads with tears and humility. According to the following text, the king extends the golden scepter to her, and she then makes her formal request.

For today: when something hurts you because of what happens to others, do not stay silent or indifferent. Pray and act with humility and courage, even if you have already had a personal victory. God can use your voice to help many people.
exp.8:14:
The verse says that the Jews in Shushan came together on the fourteenth day of the month of Adar and put to death three hundred men there. Even so, they did not lay a hand on the plunder. The point is what they chose not to take, and it is worth keeping that in view as we read the rest of the story.

This verse belongs to the story of Esther. A decree had allowed the Jews to defend themselves against those who wanted to destroy them. Esther asked the king for one more day in Shushan, and the king granted it. The text stresses that they did not take plunder, which shows that they were acting in defense and not out of greed. Some readers see this as a contrast with Haman's original decree, which ordered that everything be taken from them.

For today: when you have to defend what is right, do so with limits and without seeking personal gain. Let your motives be clean, and let neither anger nor self-interest lead you to take advantage of anyone.
exp.1:16:
