This verse tells that King Ahasuerus chose Esther from among all the young women who were brought before him. He loved her more than the others, and she found kindness and approval in his eyes. So he placed the royal crown on her head and made her queen in place of Vashti. The phrase "grace and favor" means kindness, acceptance and goodwill.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, relating the events. Vashti had been removed from her place as queen, and the king was seeking to replace her. Esther, a young Jewish woman raised by her cousin Mordecai, was brought into the palace. She followed the advice of Hegai, the keeper of the women. The text does not mention God, but many readers see his care working quietly.

For today: Even when we do not see God working in an obvious way, we can trust that he cares for our lives. In the meantime, let us live with humility, attentive to good counsel and willing to serve wherever he places us.
exp.8:24:
When Esther came before the king, he ordered in writing that the wicked scheme Haman had devised against the Jews should come back upon Haman's own head. He also commanded that Haman and his sons be hanged on the gallows. "Ordered" means commanded or instructed. "Scheme" means plan.

The one speaking here is the narrator of the book, who tells how King Ahasuerus responded to Esther's request. Haman had planned to destroy the Jews and had cast lots (Pur) to choose the date. The passage explains why the Jews celebrate Purim: they remember that God, through Esther and Mordecai, delivered them. Some scholars note that the text speaks of Haman's hanging, but also of his sons, and not all agree on the details.

For today: trust that God can change unjust situations. Ask for courage to act with wisdom when someone needs your voice, as Esther did.
exp.6:4:
King Xerxes asks Esther: "Who is this, and where is the one who would devise such a scheme?" The king did not know who had planned the ruin of Esther's people, and he wants to know who he is. The question shows his surprise and his determination to find the man behind the plot.

King Xerxes speaks, surprised and indignant. Esther has just revealed to him, with great care and respect, that she and her people have been sold to be destroyed. Up to that moment Xerxes did not know that his decree affected the queen. His question opens the way for Esther to point to Haman.

For today: Esther spoke at the right moment, with respect and without fear of the truth, even at the risk of her life. When we must defend others or say something difficult, we can pray, wait for the right moment, and speak with clarity and humility.
exp.6:1:
This verse tells that on the second day, as they drink wine at the banquet, the king asks Esther once more what she wants. He promises that she will receive it, even if it is up to half the kingdom. "Petition" and "request" mean what she asks for, and "fulfilled" means it will be carried out.

The king Ahasuerus (Xerxes) speaks with Queen Esther. She had prepared a banquet and also invited Haman, the enemy of the Jews. On the first day the king had already asked her the same question, but Esther waited. Now, at the right moment, she will make known her petition to save her people.

For today: sometimes doing what is right requires patience and good timing, not only courage. Pray, ask God for wisdom, and wait for his guidance before speaking or acting in difficult situations.
exp.5:1:
In this verse, the king's officials read the court records and found a written account: Mordecai had exposed a plot. Two of the eunuchs who guarded the king's entrance, Bigthana and Teresh, had conspired to assassinate King Xerxes. Mordecai's report is what saved the king.

The narrator of the book then connects the events. The king could not sleep and asked for the records to be read to him. That reading brought him straight to this forgotten episode, which was first mentioned back in Esther 2. Mordecai was never rewarded. The text does not name God, but many readers see here his quiet care, since everything happens just before Haman asks for Mordecai's death.

For today: do good even when no one thanks you. God sees what others forget, and he can bring the right moment to what you did faithfully.
exp.8:31:
So Esther's decree gave firm support to these regulations about Purim, and they were written into the record. This verse says that an order from Queen Esther gave firm backing to what had been set up about the festival of Purim. It was also written into the record. The word "decree" means an authoritative order or command. "Confirmed" means that she gave it validity and backing. "Written into the record" means it was put in writing, though it is not known with certainty which record is meant.

Here the narrator of the book of Esther is speaking. Mordecai had already sent letters to the Jews throughout the kingdom so that they would observe Purim every year. Now Esther, as queen, supports that decision with her authority. In this way the festival would not be something passing, but a lasting reminder that God took care of his people.

For today: let us not allow the memories of God's faithfulness to fade. Write down the occasions when God helped you, and share them with your family so that you can give thanks together.
exp.1:8:
Hegai, the official in charge of the young women, was pleased with Esther and showed her his favor. He quickly provided her with beauty treatments and a special diet, and he assigned her seven select maidservants from the palace. He also moved her and her maidservants to the best place in the harem. Here "beauty treatments" refers to the care and preparations used to enhance a woman's appearance, and "quickly" means without delay.

This is part of the account in which the king looks for a new queen and gathers many young women in Susa. Esther, an orphan raised by her cousin Mordecai, is brought into the palace. The narrator reports these events without speaking of God directly; many readers see his care behind these happenings, though the text does not say so.

For today: even in foreign or difficult places, God can give us unexpected favor and support. Live with integrity and gratitude, and trust that He works even when we cannot clearly see it.
exp.4:12:
Haman says that although he has riches, children, honor, and a special place with the king and queen, none of it gives him any satisfaction as long as he sees Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king's gate. "None of this satisfies me" means that none of it brings him contentment or joy. The king's gate was the place where Mordecai carried on his business, and he would not bow down to Haman.

Haman speaks to his friends and to his wife Zeresh, after leaving Esther's banquet. He is proud, but his pride is also wounded. One man who does not give him honor spoils everything for him. This leads him to accept the plan to hang Mordecai.

For today: when pride and envy rule us, no blessing is enough. It is wise to be thankful for what God has given us and to let go of our resentments before they grow and destroy us.
exp.0:6:
This verse tells that at the banquet of King Ahasuerus, the drinks were served in golden goblets, and each goblet had a different design. The royal wine also flowed freely, in great quantity, and reflected the king's generous bounty.

The author describes here the feast that Ahasuerus held in Susa, the capital. The narrator does the talking; the scene shows the enormous wealth of the king. Many readers see the account as setting the stage for what follows: a kingdom full of power and luxury, but also full of pride. God is not named in this book, although his care becomes visible later on.

For today: wealth and spectacle are impressive, but they are not the most valuable things. Let us ask God for a grateful and generous heart, one that uses what it has to bless others and not to show off.
exp.4:10:
Here Haman gathers his friends and his wife Zeresh, and begins to boast. He recounts to them his glorious wealth, his many sons, and all the ways the king had honored him and promoted him over the other officials and servants.

Haman had just left Queen Esther's banquet happy, but he was filled with rage when he saw that Mordecai would not bow down before him. At home, he looks for applause to soothe his wounded pride. The next verse shows that, even with so much glory, he could not be at peace.

For today: riches, fame, and achievements do not fill the heart. If we depend on the approval of others, any slight will take away our peace. Let us seek our worth in God, who gives humility and rest.
exp.3:8:
So Hathach went back and relayed Mordecai's response to Esther. The phrase "went back" and the word "relayed" carry the meaning of bringing her the message. In the text her name appears as Esther, and the Mordecai in this passage is the same man readers already know.

Hathach was a servant of the king whom Esther had sent to find out why Mordecai was dressed in mourning. Mordecai, Esther's cousin and guardian, sent her word of the decree that threatened the Jews. Hathach acted as the messenger between the two, because Esther could not go out to speak with him herself. This is the step before the difficult decision she must now make.

For today: sometimes God uses ordinary people who carry a message faithfully. We can be like Hathach: passing on honestly what others need to hear, and opening the way for someone to act with courage.
exp.0:7:
This verse says that at King Ahasuerus's banquet, the king ordered that no limit be placed on the drinking. The officers of his household were told to serve each man whatever he desired. The phrase "no limit" shows how generous and open the king's order was. So each guest could drink as much as he wanted, and no one was held to a set amount.

The book of Esther tells what happened in the kingdom of Persia. Here the narrator describes a huge and very luxurious feast that lasted many days. It shows the power and wealth of the king. This order about drinking was unusual, and the Bible does not explain why the king gave it. So it is best not to claim more than the text says.

For today: freedom and respect matter. No one should pressure others to do what they do not want to do, whether at the table or in life. We can make sure that those who are with us feel at ease and respected.
exp.8:27:
This verse says that the days of Purim were to be remembered and celebrated everywhere: by every generation, in every family, province, and city. The phrase "should not fail to be observed among the Jews" means the feast would never stop being kept among them. "Descendants" means the children and grandchildren who would follow. The idea is that each generation would keep the memory alive.

The story of Esther tells how the Jewish people in the Persian empire were saved from a plan to destroy them. Here the author explains how the Jews, together with Esther and Mordecai, established a yearly feast to remember that deliverance. Purim takes its name from "pur," the lot that was cast to choose the date of the planned attack.

For today: do not let God's kindnesses be forgotten. You can write down or tell within your family how God helped you in difficult moments, so that younger ones learn to trust him.
exp.1:17:
Then the king held a great banquet, Esther's banquet, for all his officials and servants. He proclaimed a tax holiday in the provinces and gave gifts worthy of the king's bounty. The text gives no exact details about how the tax holiday was carried out, but it shows the king sharing his good fortune with his officials and with the people across his realm.

No one speaks in this verse; the narrator is telling the story. Esther has just been made queen in place of Vashti. The king celebrates with a public banquet and gestures of kindness toward the people. What the book does not yet reveal is how God will use this place of Esther's later on, since God's name does not appear anywhere in the book.

For today: when we receive a blessing or a new position, we can use it to benefit others, not only to enjoy it. And we can trust that God works even in what seems ordinary and everyday.
exp.3:15:
Esther asks Mordecai to gather all the Jews who can be found in Susa and to fast for her for three days, not eating or drinking, day or night. She and her maidens will fast the same way. Afterward she will go to the king, even though it is against the law. She declares, "And if I perish, I perish!" meaning she accepts the risk of dying.

Esther speaks from the palace in Susa. Mordecai had told her not to keep silent, because the Jewish people were facing destruction. Going to the king without being called could cost her her life. The text does not mention God, but the fasting suggests they were seeking help beyond what was human.

For today: before a difficult decision, do not act alone or in a rush. Ask others to pray with you, seek God with humility, and then take the right step, even when it costs you.
exp.1:4:
Mordecai is introduced here: a Jewish man who lived in Susa, at the citadel, a city where the king of Persia stayed. His ancestors are named as Jair, Shimei, and Kish, and he is identified as being from the tribe of Benjamin. "Jewish man" refers to a man of Jewish descent, and "citadel" refers to the fortified part of the city where the royal palace stood.

The narrator of the book introduces a key character. Jews were living far from their land after the exile. The following verse says that someone from his family was taken captive from Jerusalem. It is not entirely clear whether it refers to Mordecai or to Kish, and scholars explain it in different ways.

God can use ordinary people who live far from home or in difficult circumstances. Wherever you find yourself today, be faithful and honor your origin and your faith, because God can work through you.
exp.8:4:
This verse says that the Jews defeated all their enemies with violence: the sword, killing, and destruction. "Put to the sword" means struck down with a weapon, and "destroying" means bringing them to ruin. The phrase "they did as they pleased to those who hated them" means they acted freely against those who had attacked them.

It is part of the story of Esther. The narrator tells of the day on which, according to Haman's decree, the enemies were going to destroy the Jews. The king allowed the Jews to defend themselves. The officials supported them out of fear of Mordecai. The text describes what happened; it does not say that God approved of every act. Interpreters discuss how to understand the harshness of this passage.

For today: let us learn to trust that God cares for his people, but let us seek to defend ourselves and to defend others with justice, without revenge or cruelty.
exp.3:4:
This verse tells how Esther, the queen, summoned Hathach, one of the king's eunuchs who had been appointed to serve her, and sent him to Mordecai to learn what was troubling him and why. The verse's wording makes clear that her purpose was to find out the cause of his distress.

Esther then sees her cousin Mordecai's grief, since he was dressed in mourning because the king had issued a decree against the Jews. She felt concern, but she did not yet know the reason behind it. So she sends someone she trusts to ask, rather than assuming.

When someone suffers near us, it is not enough to feel sorry or to send a gift. It is wise to draw close, ask with kindness, and listen to the whole story before acting.
exp.3:5:
He says that Hathach, a eunuch in the king's service, went out to meet Mordecai. He found him in the city square, in front of the king's gate. The phrase "So Hathach went out" means "then Hathach went out," and "city square" refers to an open, public space within the city.

Esther had just learned that Mordecai was dressed in sackcloth as a sign of mourning. Since he refused the clothing she had sent him, she sent Hathach, a man she trusted, to find out what was happening and why. The verse tells how that order was carried out. Mordecai was still near the king's gate, though in mourning clothes he could not enter it.

When someone is suffering, quick solutions, like the clothing Esther sent, are sometimes not enough. We need to draw near, listen, and understand the problem at its root. Ask with interest and listen with patience.
exp.4:9:
Esther 5:10 says that Haman held back and did nothing against Mordecai at that moment. He went home and called for his friends and his wife Zeresh. The word for "restrained himself" means he controlled himself and kept his feelings in check. The phrase "called for" means he summoned them to come together and gather around him.

The narrator tells what happens after Esther invited Haman to a banquet with the king. Haman left happy, but he was filled with rage when he saw that Mordecai would not bow down before him. Although he restrained himself, his anger was still alive. He wants to vent to his family and friends, where he will boast of his riches and his honor.

For today: holding back anger is not the same as healing it. Haman kept quiet, but his pride kept growing. When something bothers us, let us bring it to God in prayer and seek wise counsel, not from those who only feed our pride.
exp.3:11:
This verse is very brief: it tells us that Esther's words were passed on to Mordecai. "Relayed" here means they were reported or carried back to him.

Mordecai had asked Esther to speak with the king to save the Jews from the sentence of death. Esther, through Hatach, explained that entering before the king without being called could cost her life, and that she had not been called to the king for thirty days. She was not refusing out of coldness, but was honestly describing the real danger.

For today: when God places us before a difficult decision, there is nothing wrong with honestly expressing our fears. What matters is not to remain there, but to keep listening, to seek wise counsel, and to ask for the courage to obey.
exp.1:0:
Esther 2:1 says that some time later, when the anger of King Xerxes had subsided, he remembered Vashti, what she had done, and what had been decreed against her. The word "subsided" here means that his anger had died down and settled. The phrase "what had been decreed against her" refers to the order to remove her from her place as queen.

Context: the narrator of the book tells what happened in the palace of Persia. In chapter 1, Vashti refused to come before the king, and he, angry, removed her from her position. Here the text does not say whether he felt sadness, regret, or simply remembered. His servants notice his mood and propose that they search for a new queen.

For today: decisions made in anger often bring consequences that we later regret. Before acting while angry, it is wise to wait, pray, and think calmly. God can also work in the middle of difficult situations, even when we cannot yet see it.
exp.8:28:
This verse says that Queen Esther, daughter of Abihail, and Mordecai the Jew wrote with full authority a second letter to confirm the feast of Purim. The phrase "with full authority" means with firmness and power, and the word "confirm" means to make something firmly settled.

The book of Esther tells how God rescued the Jews from Haman's plan to destroy them. After that victory, Esther and Mordecai wanted the people never to forget what had happened. For that reason they put the yearly celebration in writing and sent it to all the provinces. Although God's name does not appear in this book, many see Him acting behind the events.

For today: remembering what God has done for us is important. We can write down or tell about the times God helped us, to thank Him and to encourage our family to trust Him.
exp.9:1:
It says that all of Mordecai's powerful and magnificent accomplishments, together with the full account of the greatness to which the king raised him, are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Media and Persia. "Chronicles" refers to records kept year by year. The question "are they not written?" invites the reader to check it, as if to say: "This is on record in the royal archives."

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Esther, closing the story. After mentioning the taxes imposed by King Ahasuerus, he notes that Mordecai was second in authority to him. We do not know for certain whether that Persian chronicle book survives today; the text mentions it only as a reference.

For today: a person's true worth lies not only in power but in using it for the good of others, as Mordecai did, seeking the welfare of his people. Strive to serve with what God has given you.
exp.8:30:
This verse says that the days of Purim were to be kept each year on their set dates. Mordecai and Queen Esther had established it, and the people agreed to keep it for themselves and for their descendants. The feast would also mark the times of fasting and lamentation, which were days of sorrow and crying out for help.

The narrator of the book tells how Mordecai and Esther wrote a second letter to the Jews in the one hundred and twenty-seven provinces of the kingdom. They wanted Purim to be firmly established as a lasting custom. The Jews had been saved from a plan to destroy them, and this feast would keep that memory alive. The text gives no further details about how the fasting was done, only that it would be remembered.

For today: when God delivers us from a difficulty, it is good to remember it on purpose. We can write a prayer of thanksgiving, tell our children what God did, or set aside a day to give thanks. In this way faith passes from one generation to the next.
exp.8:15:
The verse tells us that the other Jews living in the king's provinces, far from the capital, also came together to defend themselves. They gained relief from their enemies and killed seventy-five thousand of those who hated them. Even so, they did not lay a hand on the plunder. The phrase "they did not lay a hand on the plunder" means they did not take advantage of the spoils.

The speaker is the narrator of the book of Esther. Haman had planned to destroy the Jews, and the king allowed them to defend themselves. The account stresses that they acted to survive and not for gain. Some scholars see in this a sign that their motive was not greed.

For today: when we defend what is right, let us guard our hearts. We can act with firmness without seeking personal benefit. Let us ask ourselves: "Am I seeking justice or my own advantage?"
exp.6:5:
Here Esther clearly names the guilty person: the adversary and enemy is this wicked man, Haman. "Adversary" refers to someone who opposes others and seeks to do them harm. Haman stood in terror before the king and queen, overcome with fear and not knowing what to do.

Esther speaks at the banquet she prepared for King Ahasuerus. Up to that moment he did not know that she was a Jew, nor that her people were condemned by a decree that Haman had promoted. After praying and preparing herself, Esther finally reveals the truth and asks for justice, risking her own life.

For today: sometimes we must speak with courage and truth in the face of injustice, even when it is frightening. We can do so with respect and wisdom, trusting that God cares for his people and can use our voice at the right moment.
exp.8:26:
This verse says that the Jews firmly committed themselves to keep these two days every year, as they had been written down and at their set time. "Descendants" is the meaning of "seed" here. "Those who join themselves to them" refers to people who became part of their community. The phrase "should not fail" means the custom would never be allowed to lapse.

The one who speaks is the narrator of the book. He tells how, after God rescued them from Haman's plot, the Jews agreed to keep the festival of Purim. They wanted their children and future generations to remember that deliverance and never forget it.

For today: remember with gratitude what God has done for us. We can build simple habits, such as giving thanks together as a family or telling our children how God helped us, so that faith and memory are passed on to the next generation.
exp.0:21:
Esther 1:22 tells us that King Ahasuerus sent letters to all the provinces of his kingdom. Each province received its message in its own script, and each people received it in their own language. The decree proclaimed that every man should be master of his own household.

After Queen Vashti refused to appear before the king at a banquet, Memucan, one of his counselors, feared that other wives would do the same. The king followed his advice and issued this decree. The book only reports the event and does not approve of it. Many readers see in the scene the pride and insecurity of the Persian court.

Today we can notice that ruling the home by decree does not produce true respect. The Bible teaches that the home is built up with love, humility, and mutual service (Ephesians 5:21). Let us ask God for wisdom to treat our family with respect.
exp.1:10:
This verse says that every day Mordecai walked back and forth in front of the courtyard of the harem. He wanted to learn how Esther was doing and what was happening to her. The phrase "back and forth" means he kept pacing up and down, and "what was happening to her" means what was going on with her.

The narrator is the one telling us this. Esther, a young Jewish woman, had been taken into the Persian palace, and Mordecai, her relative who had raised her, had asked her not to reveal her people. He could not go inside, but he stayed close by to watch over her well-being. Many interpret this as a father's care, though the text does not say more.

Today we can learn to steadily stand by those we love, even when we cannot control their situation. A phone call, a visit, or a daily prayer can be a real way of caring.
exp.6:8:
Here the account tells how Harbonah, one of the eunuchs attending the king, reports to him that Haman had a gallows built about fifty cubits high, roughly twenty-three meters, at his house, intended for Mordecai, the man who had given the report that saved the king. A gallows is a tall wooden structure used for hanging someone. The king responds, "Hang him on it!"

Harbonah speaks at the moment when Haman is already condemned because of his attitude toward the queen. Mordecai had earlier uncovered a plot against the king, and Haman wanted to kill him out of pride and resentment. Scholars do not know the exact height of the gallows, but the text emphasizes how excessive it was.

Today we can learn that the harm planned against others can turn back on the one who prepares it. Instead of feeding resentment, let us trust in God, who sees injustice and knows how to act in his own time.
exp.1:19:
Esther had still not told anyone what people she came from or who her relatives were, because Mordecai had told her to keep it secret. She obeyed his command, just as she had done when he cared for her as a child.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Esther was already queen of Persia, but Mordecai, her cousin and guardian, was still guiding her. The text does not explain why he asked for that silence. Some think he wanted to protect her, and others think he wanted to wait for the right moment. What we do see is that, shortly afterward, Mordecai uncovers a plot against the king.

For today: even when we reach places of success or responsibility, it is wise to stay humble and willing to listen to the advice of wise people. That attitude protects us and can prepare us for whatever God does next.
exp.8:12:
Esther asks the king for two things: that the Jews in Susa may have one more day to carry out the edict they were permitted to act on the day before, and that the bodies of Haman's ten sons be hanged on the gallows. "Susa" is the capital city, and "if it pleases the king" means "if it seems good to the king." Hanging the sons probably means displaying their bodies after they were already dead, though some read it differently.

Queen Esther is speaking. King Ahasuerus has just told her about the five hundred men killed in Susa, and he offers to grant her another request. Haman had planned to destroy the Jews, and the decree could not be cancelled, so they had permission to defend themselves. Esther asks for more time, probably because enemies were still in the city.

For today: Esther used her position with courage to protect her people. You too can use your influence to defend the vulnerable, but this scene is a historical account, not a model of revenge. Jesus calls us to love even our enemies.
exp.0:20:
This verse says that Memucan's proposal pleased King Ahasuerus and his princes, and that the king put it into practice. The word "pleased" here means that the proposal was welcome to them and seemed good in their eyes. The phrase "this counsel" refers to what Memucan had advised, that is, his recommendation.

The context is this: Queen Vashti had refused to appear before the king during a banquet. Memucan, one of the counselors, feared that other women would follow her example and proposed removing her from her position. His advice came from anger and from fear of losing authority, not from a search for justice. The Bible here recounts what happened without approving of it.

For today: before accepting advice, let us ask what motivates it. Decisions made out of pride or anger, even when they please many people, can cause harm. Let us seek the wisdom of God, which is humble and peaceable (James 3:17).
exp.8:22:
This verse says that the Jews agreed to continue the custom they had already started, just as Mordecai had written to them. "Agreed" means they willingly accepted it and committed themselves to keeping it each year.

The one speaking here is the narrator of the book. Mordecai had written letters so that the people would remember each year their rescue from Haman's plans. The festival, called Purim, was established so that they would not forget how their sorrow turned into joy. The verses that follow explain the reason for the festival.

For today: let us not allow the memory of what God has done for us to be lost. We can set aside regular moments, such as a family meal or a prayer of thanksgiving, to remember his blessings and share joy with others, especially those in need.
exp.8:5:
This verse tells that in the citadel of Susa, the Jews killed and destroyed five hundred men. Susa was the capital of the Persian kingdom, and "destroyed" here means they put an end to these men, who had made themselves enemies of the Jews.

The book of Esther relates that, by a decree of the king, the Jews were able to defend themselves on the day their enemies planned to attack them. Here the narrator of the book speaks, describing what happened. Mordecai already had authority, and for that reason the people were not overcome. Some scholars see this as self-defense in the midst of a real threat; others feel uneasy about the number of dead. The text only reports what happened.

For today: God cares for his people in times of danger, but we must take this with seriousness and humility, without seeking revenge. We can trust God and ask him for wisdom to defend what is right without hatred.
exp.4:0:
On the third day, Esther put on her royal robes and stood in the inner court of the palace, across from the king's quarters. The king was sitting on his royal throne in the royal courtroom, facing the entrance. The verse names the throne as the royal throne, and the royal courtroom is the king's hall within the palace.

The narrator tells us this. Esther had asked the Jews to fast for three days on her behalf (Esther 4:16), because entering the king's presence without being called could cost her her life. Now, after those days have passed, she takes the step. The text does not say what she felt, but it is clear that she acts with courage.

For today: when you have to face something difficult, prepare yourself with prayer and the support of others, and then take the step. Courage is not the absence of fear, but moving forward after you have prepared.
exp.2:2:
The king's servants who guarded the palace gate asked Mordecai why he was disobeying the king's command. The word "disobey" means to refuse to follow an order or to break a command.

These were the officials who worked at the king's gate, where Mordecai also served. The king had ordered everyone to bow down before Haman, but Mordecai did not do so. The text does not explain his reason here; it only says later that he had told them he was a Jew. Some think he acted for religious reasons, others because of the hostility between his people and the Agagites, and the Bible does not make this clear in this passage.

Some convictions bring pressure, and at times others do not understand our firmness. Let us ask God for wisdom to remain faithful with humility and courage, trusting that he cares for us even when it costs us.
exp.7:13:
The king's couriers rode out quickly to carry the new law, mounted on royal horses. The phrase "pressed on" means they were driven forward by the urgency of the king's command. The verse says the edict was issued in the citadel of Susa, the capital city. The law was made known there, and from there it went out across the kingdom.

The one who tells the story is the author of the book of Esther. Earlier, Haman had obtained a decree to destroy the Jews, and a decree of the king could not be revoked. So the king, at the request of Esther and Mordecai, authorized another decree that allowed the Jews to defend themselves. There was little time, and that is why there was such haste.

For today: when you have good news or help that others need, do not put it off. A word of encouragement, a piece of advice, or a prayer offered in time can ease someone who lives with fear.
exp.6:6:
This verse says that the king got up from his wine in a fury and went out into the palace garden. Haman stayed behind to beg Queen Esther to spare his life, because he realized that the king was planning a terrible fate for him. The "garden" here is the palace grounds, and the king's "fury" was a strong rage. In this verse, "beg" means to plead earnestly.

Esther had just accused Haman before King Ahasuerus of being the enemy who wanted to destroy her people. The king went out to cool down and think. Haman, with no way out, tried to plead with the one person who could speak for him, the very woman he had threatened.

For today: sooner or later, what we sow catches up with us. Haman lived with pride and wickedness, and in the end he had no one to turn to. It is worth living with humility and justice, and asking for forgiveness in time, before the crisis arrives.
exp.5:2:
Here King Ahasuerus asks what honor or reward Mordecai received for having uncovered a plot against the king's life. "Honor" and "dignity" refer to recognition and reward. The attendants answer that nothing has been done for him, meaning no one has rewarded him.

The king could not sleep, and he ordered that the book of the chronicles be read to him. There he found that Mordecai had reported two eunuchs who had wanted to kill him. The king realizes that this debt was left unpaid. Shortly afterward Haman arrives to ask for Mordecai's death. The text does not mention God, but many readers see here his quiet care in a sleepless night.

For today: God can watch over the details of our lives without our noticing. Do good faithfully, even when no one acknowledges it, and trust that God sees and knows how to act in his time.
exp.8:17:
This verse tells that the Jews of Susa, the capital of the Persian kingdom, gathered together on the thirteenth and fourteenth days of the month of Adar to defend themselves against their enemies. On the fifteenth day they rested and made it a day of feasting and joy. The name "Susa" refers to the city known in the Hebrew text as Shushan, and "gathered together" means that they organized themselves and came together.

Here the narrator of the book of Esther speaks. He describes how the danger that threatened the Jewish people because of Haman's decree came to an end. The Jews in the provinces rested on the fourteenth day, but those in Susa fought one more day and rested on the fifteenth. That is why the feast of Purim is celebrated on different dates depending on the place, as the text that follows explains.

For today: after a struggle or a difficult trial, God invites us to rest and give thanks. Taking time to celebrate what he has done helps us remember his faithfulness.
exp.5:4:
The king's attendants tell him that Haman is standing in the court. King Ahasuerus, not knowing why Haman has come, gives a single command: "Bring him in." The "court" was the outer courtyard of the palace, and the "attendants" were the officials who served the king.

The king could not sleep, and he had asked for the records of the kingdom to be read to him. There he learned that Mordecai had uncovered a plot against his life and had never been rewarded. Just then Haman arrived, very early in the morning, to ask that Mordecai be hanged on the gallows he had prepared. The attendants only report who is outside; they do not know what is about to happen.

God is not named in the book of Esther, but many see his care in these well-timed events. Today we can remember that God keeps working even when we cannot see it. If you are going through an unjust or confusing situation, trust that he can change things at the right moment, and in the meantime keep doing what is right with patience.
exp.3:16:
The verse says that Mordecai went and did all that Esther had instructed him. The phrase "went and did" describes him simply carrying out what she asked, and the wording "all that Esther had instructed him" shows that he followed her directions fully. In other words, Mordecai obeyed Esther's instructions without arguing.

The narrator tells what happened after Esther's message. The Jewish people were in danger because of a decree of death. Esther decided to approach the king without being summoned, which could cost her her life. She asked that all the Jews in Susa fast with her for three days. Mordecai, who had once given orders to her, now obeys her. This shows a change of roles and his trust in her.

For today: when someone takes a brave step and asks for support, let us help with humility. Sometimes God calls us to follow others, even though we may once have been the ones leading. Let us pray and walk alongside them in faith.
exp.0:8:
Queen Vashti also gave a banquet of her own, but only for the women, in the royal palace of King Xerxes. While the king was hosting a great feast for the men, she was entertaining the guests among the women. The word "also" here means "too" or "in the same way."

The Book of Esther tells the story of what happened in the Persian empire. Here the narrator describes the king's feast, which lasted many days and had plenty of wine and luxury. This detail sets up what follows: when the king is cheerful from the wine, he sends for Vashti, and from there the story takes a very important turn.

For today: decisions made in the middle of a feast or of excess can have serious consequences. This invites us to act with calm and wisdom, and to remember that God works even in disordered situations.
exp.9:2:
This verse says that Mordecai the Jew was second only to King Xerxes in importance. He was outstanding among the Jews and highly favored by most of his fellow countrymen. He sought the good of his people and spoke peace to all of his countrymen. The phrase "highly favored" means well received and held dear, and "countrymen" means the people of his nation.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Esther, who closes the story. Mordecai had helped save the Jews from Haman's decree of destruction. Now the account shows that his power did not end in personal pride, but was used to protect and encourage his people. The author is not named with certainty.

For today: if God gives us influence, at work, in the family, or in the church, let us use it to serve and to promote peace, not to show off. Let us seek the good of others with words that build up.
exp.0:19:
The verse says that when the king's edict is issued, it will be heard throughout his vast kingdom, and that as a result all women, from the least to the greatest, will honor their husbands. "Honor" means to show respect or hold someone in high regard. The phrase "vast kingdom" points to how wide the king's realm is.

The one speaking is Memucan, one of the king's advisers. Queen Vashti had refused to come to the king at a banquet, and Memucan feared that other women would follow her example. His proposal comes from fear and wounded pride, and the text only reports that the king accepted it. It does not say that God approved it.

For today: true respect is not produced by orders or fear. It is earned through love, humility, and good treatment. As Ephesians 5:21 says, the Bible invites us to submit to one another out of reverence for Christ.
exp.8:9:
This verse ends the list of the ten sons of Haman, who were killed on the day the Jews defended themselves. They are named as the sons of Haman son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews. One detail stands out: the Jews did not lay a hand on the plunder, meaning they did not take the possessions of the dead.

The narrator of the book tells how the king's decree allowing the Jews to defend themselves was carried out. Haman had planned to destroy them. The Jews did not act for gain, but for defense. This is repeated three times in the chapter, and so it seems important to the author. Taking plunder would have shown greed, and the text makes clear that they did not do so.

For today: even when we are right or defending something just, let us watch our motives. Let us not use difficult situations to gain something for ourselves.
exp.2:6:
This verse tells that, in the first month of the twelfth year of King Xerxes, Haman had the Pur, that is, the lot, cast before him, as if they were dice or stones. He did this day after day and month after month, to determine a day and month. The lot fell on the twelfth month, the month of Adar.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Haman was filled with rage because Mordecai would not bow down to him. So he sought to destroy all the Jews in the kingdom. To decide when to do it, he used the lot, as was done in that culture to seek a favorable time.

For today: hatred can plan with great care, but it does not have the last word. Haman left his plan to chance, but God continues to guide the story. Entrust your worries to God and not to chance.
exp.7:16:
Wherever the king's new edict arrived, the Jews celebrated with joy, gladness, feasting, and celebration. The verse itself describes "joy and gladness" among the Jews, so the celebration was real and widespread. Also, many people from among the surrounding population came to identify themselves with the Jews, because the fear of the Jews had fallen on them.

The narrator of the book of Esther tells what happened after the king allowed the Jews to defend themselves against Haman's plan to destroy them. Their lives had been in danger, and now they were delivered. Scholars are not sure whether those people truly converted or only sought to protect themselves.

Today we can remember that God cares for his people even when he is not obviously seen. When he delivers us from something difficult, it is worth pausing, giving thanks, and celebrating with others.
exp.0:2:
In the third year of his reign, King Xerxes held a feast for all his officials and servants. The military leaders of Persia and Media were there, along with the nobles and princes of the provinces. "Held a feast" means that he hosted a grand celebration. "The military leaders of Persia and Media" refers to his leaders and army commanders.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, presenting King Xerxes (often identified with Xerxes I, though this is a common identification, not a certain one). He gathered his leaders to display the splendor of his power, as the following verses describe. The account sets the stage for the scene in which Esther will appear.

For today: it is easy to impress others with what we have or accomplish. But human power passes away. We can ask ourselves whether we seek our own glory or whether we use what God has given us to serve and honor Him.
exp.9:0:
This verse says that King Xerxes imposed a tax throughout his whole kingdom, reaching even to its farthest shores. "Imposed tribute" means he required a payment of money to the government. The phrase "even to its farthest shores" points to the distant regions of his empire, the lands at the edge of the sea.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking, not a character. After telling how the Jewish people were saved, the book briefly shows the king's power. It then highlights Mordecai, who became second only to the king and used his position to seek the good of his people. Why the tax is mentioned is not clear; some believe it shows the stability of the kingdom.

For today: power and money pass away, but what remains is using our influence, great or small, to serve others and to pursue peace.
exp.0:17:
This verse says that the noble women of Persia and Media, once they hear what Queen Vashti did, will talk about it with the king's officials. The result would be "much contempt and wrath": the wives would look down on their husbands, and the husbands would become angry. "Noble women" means the women of high standing, and "contempt" means a lack of respect.

The speaker is Memucan, one of King Ahasuerus's advisers. Vashti refused to appear before the king at a banquet. Memucan exaggerates the situation, fearing that the event will weaken the authority of men, and he proposes removing her as queen. This is the advice of a man worried about his own position, not a teaching from God.

For today: be careful not to let the fear of losing status or control lead us into exaggerated reactions. Respect in the home is not won through rules or forced demands, but through love, honest conversation, and dignified treatment.
exp.1:9:
Esther had not revealed her people or her family. She kept this to herself because her cousin Mordecai, who had raised her, had instructed her not to reveal it. The word "revealed" in the Berean Standard Bible means to make known or to tell openly.

The book presents this as a fact. Esther, a young Jewish woman, now lives in the palace of the Persian king, in Susa, among many young women gathered for the king. Mordecai gives her this instruction, but the text does not explain his reasons. Some think he wanted to protect her from prejudice against the Jews; others think he was preparing for what would come later. We cannot know this for certain.

There are times when God calls us to wisdom and not to speak about everything right away. Listening to the advice of wise and trustworthy people helps us decide when to keep quiet and when to speak, trusting that God is at work even in what we do not understand.
exp.8:13:
This verse says that King Ahasuerus approved what Esther asked for. The order was issued in Susa, the capital, and Haman's ten sons were hanged. "Susa" is the city where the events take place, and "hanged" means their bodies were put on display on the gallows, probably after they had died, though the text does not make this clear.

Esther speaks with the king after the first day of fighting, when the Jews defended themselves against Haman's decree that sought their destruction. She asks for one more day and for the public display of Haman's sons. Some believe this was a signal meant to discourage other enemies; the text does not explain more. Note that the Jews did not take any plunder.

For today: this passage reminds us that unjust evil has consequences, but it also invites us to seek justice without greed or personal revenge. Let us trust that God cares for his people, and ask him for wisdom to act with righteousness.
exp.1:21:
Mordecai learned of the plot by two royal officers to kill the king. He reported it to Queen Esther, and she warned the king, making clear that the news came from Mordecai.

The words "when he learned of the plot" mean that Mordecai found out about the scheme. "Reported" means that he passed the information on, and "on Mordecai's behalf" shows that Esther gave him the credit.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, without quoting anyone. Mordecai was sitting at the palace gate, a place where official matters were handled. Esther still kept silent about her Jewish origin, as he had asked her to. This event was recorded in the chronicles of the kingdom, and later it will become very important in the story.

For today: when someone helps you or contributes something valuable, acknowledge it honestly and give credit to the one who deserves it. Doing what is right, even when no one notices, is never lost.
exp.5:6:
Haman answers King Ahasuerus with the very words the king used to ask him: "For the man whom the king is delighted to honor." This is the opening of his reply, which continues in the verses that follow. Here "man" simply means a man, and "honor" refers to public recognition.

Haman is a high official of the kingdom. The king asks him how to honor someone, but does not say who. Haman, thinking it must be himself, says to himself: "Whom would the king desire to honor more than me?" That is why he asks for very great honors. In truth, the king wanted to honor Mordecai, the Jew whom Haman hated.

For today: pride leads us to assume things and to seek the first places. Let us rather learn to serve with humility and let God, in his time, be the one who honors us, as Proverbs 27:2 says.
exp.6:3:
Here Esther says that she and her people have been sold out to destruction, death, and annihilation. She says that if they had merely been sold as menservants and maidservants, she would have remained silent. The last sentence is difficult: it seems to say that this lesser hardship would not justify burdening the king, though some understand it in other ways.

Esther speaks before King Ahasuerus at the second banquet. Until now she had kept secret that she was Jewish. Haman, a high official, had obtained a decree to exterminate the Jews. Esther risks her life by revealing her identity and asking the king for help.

For today: when you see an injustice and have a voice or influence, do not hide. Ask God for wisdom and courage to speak with respect, at the right moment, and on behalf of those who cannot defend themselves.
exp.6:0:
This verse says that King Ahasuerus went with Haman to a dinner to share a meal with Queen Esther. "Went" means that they arrived, and "dine" here refers to a banquet, a meal with wine.

The narrator is the author of the book of Esther. Esther had already invited the king and Haman to a first banquet, and now the second takes place. She does not yet know how the king will react, but she is preparing to plead for her people, the Jews, whom Haman had condemned to death. This banquet is the key moment when she will speak.

For today: Esther did not rush or act on impulse; she waited for the right moment and prepared herself with courage. When you face a difficult situation, pray, prepare yourself, and seek wisdom before you speak or act. God can use your patience and your courage to help others.
exp.8:6:
This verse begins a list of the names of ten men whom the Jews killed in Susa, the capital. Here appear the first three: Parshandatha, Dalphon, and Aspatha. The word "including" connects this list with the five hundred men already mentioned.

The one who narrates is the author of the book of Esther. He tells what happened on the day when the enemies of the Jews intended to attack them, but King Ahasuerus had allowed them to defend themselves. These ten were sons of Haman. The texts do not explain in detail why they are named, though they perhaps show that the event was real and that the danger was brought to an end.

For today: God cares for his people in moments of threat. We can trust that he sees our struggles, and we should seek justice without letting resentment govern us.
exp.8:7:
This verse continues a list of names. Here three of Haman's ten sons appear: Poratha, Adalia, and Aridatha. In this list, it means that these sons too were killed by the Jews in Susa.

The narrator of the book of Esther recounts what happened on the day Haman had ordered the Jews destroyed. The king allowed them to defend themselves. Haman's ten sons were part of that enemy. The text emphasizes that the Jews did not take the plunder, and this suggests they acted in defense and not out of greed.

For today: when we must defend ourselves or seek justice, let us do so without greed or any desire for gain. And let us trust that God cares for his people, even when the situation is hard and painful.
exp.0:1:
This verse says that in those days, King Xerxes sat on his royal throne, and that the throne was in Susa, the citadel, the seat of government. The phrase "sat on his royal throne" describes the king being firmly in power, settled in the place of his authority. Here "throne" means the seat of the king's rule.

The book of Esther is told by a narrator who does not identify himself. Here he sets the scene: a very powerful king, with an enormous government and a royal citadel in Susa. Many believe this King Xerxes is Xerxes I of Persia, although the text does not spell that out. This introduction prepares the story that follows, in which God will act without being named directly.

For today: even when human power seems vast and secure, it does not have the final word. We can trust that God works with care even when we do not see it at first glance.
exp.5:7:
Haman tells the king what should be done for the man the king wishes to honor. He proposes that they bring a royal robe that the king himself has worn, a horse on which the king himself has ridden, and a royal crest placed on the horse's head. The wording here is close to how we would speak today, so no further explanation is needed. Some scholars understand that the crest was placed on the horse, and others that it was placed on the man; the text does not make this completely clear.

Haman speaks because the king asks him, and he believes the honor is for himself. Out of pride, he asks for the most. But the king orders that all of this be done for Mordecai, the Jew whom Haman hated.

For today: pride deceives us and makes us believe that everything revolves around us. Let us ask God for a humble heart, one that rejoices when others are honored.
exp.4:2:
Here the king asks Esther what she wants and what she is requesting from him. He promises to give her up to half of the kingdom. The king speaks after Esther came into his presence without being called, which could have cost her her life. He extended the golden scepter and so showed her his favor. The phrase "up to half of the kingdom" seems to be an expression of generosity rather than a literal offer. Esther does not yet ask for what she truly needs, but instead invites the king and Haman to a banquet. Many understand that she acts with caution and wisdom, although the text does not explain all her motives.

When you face something difficult, pray and ask God for direction before acting. Sometimes wisdom consists in waiting for the right moment and speaking with prudence, trusting that God works in every step.
exp.6:7:
When the king came back from the palace garden to the banquet hall, he found Haman falling onto the couch where Queen Esther was reclining. The king asked whether Haman would really assault the queen while the king was still in the palace. The king's words show that he took the scene as an assault or an act of violence. As soon as the king finished speaking, they covered Haman's face, a sign that he was condemned and sentenced.

Esther had just accused Haman of being the enemy of her people. The king left in anger, and Haman stayed behind begging for his life. When he fell onto the couch, he was probably trying to plead for mercy, but the king saw it differently. Interpreters agree that Haman did not intend to attack her, though the king took it that way.

For today: pride and wickedness may seem powerful, but sooner or later they are exposed. We can trust that God is at work even when we cannot see it, and act with courage and truth, as Esther did.
exp.8:3:
This verse says that Mordecai exercised great power in the palace. His reputation spread through every province, and his influence kept growing. The phrase "as he became more and more powerful" describes his rising authority over time.

Here the narrator of the book of Esther speaks. He explains why no one dared to oppose the Jews on the day they could defend themselves: the officials of the kingdom knew that Mordecai was a respected authority, and for that reason they supported them. The text shows a complete change, since Mordecai had been threatened with death and now he was honored.

For today: God can change very difficult situations and use faithful people in places of influence. If you are in a position of responsibility, use it with integrity and to protect others, not only for your own benefit.
exp.0:4:
When these days had ended, the king held a second feast, this time lasting seven days. It took place in the garden court of the royal palace. He invited all the people in the citadel of Susa, from the least to the greatest.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Esther. He tells the events concerning King Ahasuerus. His purpose is to show the enormous wealth and power of the king, and to set the stage for the appearance of Esther later on.

For today: luxury and human power impress, but they do not last. We can enjoy what God gives us with gratitude, without placing our security in it, but in Him, who governs even behind the scenes.
exp.2:14:
The couriers left quickly, urged on by the king's command, to carry the edict against the Jews. The decree was also issued in the citadel of Susa. "Spurred on" means pushed forward in a hurry. "Confusion" means turmoil and distress. Meanwhile, the king and Haman sat down to drink, but the city of Susa was in turmoil.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Haman, a high official, had persuaded the king to sign an order to destroy the Jews, out of his hatred for Mordecai. The contrast is strong: two men drink together calmly, while ordinary people are filled with fear at such injustice.

For today: do not be indifferent to the pain of others. Even when others live at ease, you can care about those who suffer, pray for them, and help in whatever way you can. God sees what seems hidden.
exp.2:4:
What it says: Haman saw that Mordecai would not bow down or pay him homage, and he was filled with rage. The phrases "bow down" and "pay him homage" describe making a deep bow, as a sign of respect and submission.

Context: The narrator tells us that the king had ordered that Haman, his high official, be honored. Mordecai, who was a Jew, refused, and the king's servants reported him. The text does not explain the exact reason for his refusal. Some think it was out of loyalty to God, others because of the history of enmity between his people and the Amalekites, since Haman is called an Agagite. This is an interpretation, not something stated clearly here.

For today: Wounded pride can grow until it becomes destructive. Before reacting with anger, let us ask God to help us calm our hearts and not let our ego guide us.
exp.0:0:
This verse opens the book of Esther by placing the story in the time of King Xerxes. It makes clear that he was the ruler over 127 provinces stretching from India to Cush. The phrase "This is what happened" simply introduces the events that follow. "Provinces" were regions governed within the empire.

The author of the book is not named, and it is not known with certainty who wrote it. It tells the events as a historical account. Many believe Xerxes is the Persian king known as Xerxes I, though this is suggested mainly by the similarity of names. The text highlights his enormous power as the setting for what follows: a vast empire in which the Jewish people lived in exile.

Although God is not mentioned directly in this book, we can learn that He works even within the great systems of human power. If today you feel small in the face of enormous situations, remember that God is not absent. You can trust that He continues to guide your story, even when you cannot clearly see His hand.
exp.4:7:
Esther tells the king that if he is pleased with her and is willing to grant what she asks, he should come with Haman to a second banquet that she will prepare for them. There she will give her answer to the king's question. "Found favor in the sight of the king" means she has made a good impression on him and has his goodwill. A "petition" is what she is asking him for. "Prepare" means she will get everything ready for the banquet.

She is Queen Esther, a young Jewish woman. King Ahasuerus has offered her up to half the kingdom, but she does not yet reveal her request. Her people are in danger because of Haman's plan. Many think she is waiting for the right moment, though the text does not fully explain her reasons.

For today: you do not always have to say everything at once. Before taking an important step, pray, think calmly, and look for the right moment and the right way, trusting that God is guiding the process.
exp.7:0:
That same day King Xerxes awarded Queen Esther the estate of Haman, the enemy of the Jews. It also says that Mordecai entered the king's presence, because Esther had revealed his relation to her. The word "awarded" in the verse above means the king formally gave the property to Esther. The word "revealed" means that she made known to the king the relationship between herself and Mordecai.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Haman had been put to death after planning the destruction of the Jewish people. According to the text, Mordecai was Esther's cousin and had raised her. Now the king acknowledges Mordecai and begins to restore what had been turned upside down. The account does not say how much the king knew before this.

For today: God can change unjust situations, and sometimes He does so through brave and sincere people. If He has placed you in a place of influence, use your voice honestly to help others.
exp.7:15:
The verse says that the Jews went through a complete change: they moved from anguish to light, that is, to hope and salvation. "Gladness" is a deep happiness, and "honor" means they were once again respected. Notice that the word "Jews" is written with a capital letter, as a name for a people.

It is the narrator of the book of Esther who tells this. The king had allowed a second decree that let the Jews defend themselves, after Haman had planned to destroy them. Mordecai had been honored, and the news reached all the provinces. The text does not name God, but many see in the story his hidden care.

For today: when God brings you out of a difficulty, do not keep the relief to yourself in silence. Stop, give thanks, and celebrate with others. And if today you are in darkness, remember that this story shows that sorrow can change.

sum.6: At the second banquet, Queen Esther asks the king to spare her life and the lives of her people, who were about to be destroyed, and she points to Haman as the enemy. The king becomes furious, Haman is disgraced, and he is hanged on the same gallows he had prepared for Mordecai. The passage shows how evil planned against others can turn back on the one who planned it.
sum.1: After the anger of King Ahasuerus had calmed down, officials searched for beautiful young virgins so that a new queen could be chosen. Esther, a young Jewish woman raised by her cousin Mordecai, was selected and won the favor of everyone who saw her. Esther kept her people a secret, just as Mordecai had asked her to. Mordecai uncovered a plot against the king and warned him, and this was recorded.
sum.4: Esther goes before the king without being summoned, and he extends his scepter to her and offers her up to half the kingdom. She only invites him to a banquet with Haman, and then to another the next day. Haman leaves happy, but his fury against Mordecai leads him to prepare a gallows.
sum.7: The king gave Esther the house of Haman, and Mordecai received the king's signet ring. Esther begged the king, weeping, to undo the decree against her people. Since the king's law could not be revoked, a new decree was sent out that allowed the Jews to defend themselves. There was great joy among them, and many people joined the Jewish community.
sum.8:
On the thirteenth day of the month of Adar, when their enemies had hoped to overpower them, the Jews fought back and won across the entire kingdom. They did not take the property of those they defeated.

Esther asked for one more day in Susa, and the ten sons of Haman were hanged.

Mordecai instructed that these days be remembered every year as Purim, with feasts, joy, gifts exchanged, and help given to the poor.
sum.3: Mordecai wept bitterly when he learned of the decree against the Jews, and through Hatach, Esther found out everything. She hesitated, because appearing before the king without being summoned could cost her her life, but Mordecai told her: "Who knows whether you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" Esther decided to fast with her people and take the risk: "If I perish, I perish."
sum.2: King Ahasuerus promoted Haman, but Mordecai, who was a Jew, refused to bow down to him. Enraged, Haman decided to destroy the entire Jewish people. He cast lots to choose the date and persuaded the king to sign a decree of extermination. The chapter shows how wounded pride can lead to terrible hatred, while the city was left shaken.
sum.9: King Ahasuerus imposed a tax on his land, reaching even to the islands of the sea, and his great accomplishments are written in the records of the kings of Media and Persia. The chapter ends by highlighting Mordecai, the Jew who became second only to the king. He was highly respected among his people because he sought their good and spoke peace to all of them.
sum.5: One night King Ahasuerus could not sleep, and when he had the chronicles read to him, he discovered that Mardochai had never been rewarded for saving the king's life. Haman, thinking that the man to be honored would be himself, proposed great honors, and the king ordered him to give them to Mardochai. Humiliated, Haman heard from his wise men that he would fall before this Jew.
sum.0: King Ahasuerus, who ruled over 127 provinces, held great banquets to display his wealth and power. When Queen Vashti refused to come before him, the king became angry and, on the advice of Memucan, issued a decree that she was no longer to come into his presence. The passage shows human pride and its consequences.
